setup: When a hagfish gets clogged up in its own defensive slime, it cleans itself off by...
answer: tying its body in a knot and sliding the knot down
detail: Hagfish are jawless, eel-like fish. Passing a knot from head to tail wipes the slime away so they don't suffocate in their own goo once the danger has passed.
source_title: University of British Columbia: Hagfish Slime Research

setup: When a hagfish releases its slime into seawater, the gloop expands to around...
answer: 10,000 times its original volume in under half a second
detail: The slime is mucus mixed with fine protein threads that unspool on contact with water. It can clog the gills of a predatory fish, buying the hagfish time to escape.
source_title: KQED Deep Look: How Hagfish Unleash a Torrent of Slime

setup: Sloth moths spend their adult lives living in a sloth's fur, but they lay their eggs...
detail: Females hop off when the sloth climbs down to the forest floor to go to the toilet. The larvae grow up in the dung, then fly up into the canopy to find a sloth of their own.

setup: Three-toed sloths risk a dangerous trip down from the trees about once a week. They make the journey in order to...
detail: Researchers think the habit feeds a little ecosystem: moths breed in the dung, then live in the fur, fertilising algae that grows there, which the sloth then eats as a dietary supplement.
source_title: Capital FM (AFP): Sloth and moth are loth to part

setup: To supplement their diet of leaves, three-toed sloths are thought to snack on...
answer: algae growing in their own fur
detail: Algae flourish in the sloth's coat, helped by nitrogen from moths that live there. A 2014 study found the same fatty, energy-rich algae in sloths' stomachs, suggesting they eat it.
source_title: Capital FM (AFP): Sloth and moth are loth to part

setup: Scientists studying Atlantic herring found the fish make a high-pitched ticking noise, which video showed was produced by...
answer: releasing bubbles of gas from their bottoms
detail: Researchers called them Fast Repetitive Tick sounds. Video analysis linked the sounds to bubbles expelled from the anal duct region.
source_title: Discover Magazine: Which animal communicates by farting?

setup: The pearlfish is a slender little fish that spends its days hiding safely inside...
detail: Sea cucumbers breathe through their rear ends, so the pearlfish waits for it to open, then slips in, sometimes tail-first in time with the host's breathing. It comes out at night to feed.
source_title: Australian Geographic: The fish that lives in a sea cucumber anus

setup: Pearlfish usually live alone inside a sea cucumber, but in the 1970s a biologist studying a single large sea cucumber found...
detail: Victor Benno Meyer-Rochow reported the record in 1977: 14 fish emerged when the sea cucumber was put in cold water, and one stayed inside. Normally a host shelters one pearlfish, or a pair.
source_title: Australian Geographic: The fish that lives in a sea cucumber anus

setup: Most pearlfish are harmless lodgers inside sea cucumbers, but some species repay the hospitality by...
detail: The Smithsonian notes that while the relationship is usually harmless, some pearlfish are parasites that eat the sea cucumber's gonads and other internal organs from the inside.
source_title: Smithsonian Ocean: Pearlfish from a Sea Cucumber

setup: Australia's Fitzroy River turtle can stay underwater for up to three weeks, because it can take in oxygen by...
detail: It is nicknamed the 'bum-breathing turtle'. Using its cloaca, it can take up to 70% of its oxygen needs straight from the water. It lives only in Queensland's Fitzroy River system.

setup: In 2020 scientists shone ultraviolet light on museum specimens of platypuses and discovered that their fur...
detail: The researchers used specimens from the Field Museum in Chicago and the University of Nebraska State Museum. The brown fur reflected bright blue-green light under UV.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine: Platypuses glow green under UV light

setup: Giraffes were long thought to be almost silent, until scientists recorded 947 hours of zoo giraffes and found that at night they...
detail: Researchers from the University of Vienna recorded giraffes at three European zoos over eight years. The low hum, around 92 hertz, was at the bottom of human hearing and was made at night.
source_title: Christian Science Monitor: You probably didn't expect giraffes to sound like this

setup: Every night, a wombat produces somewhere between 80 and 100...
detail: Researchers at Georgia Tech found the cubes form because the walls of the wombat's intestine stretch unevenly. Wombats leave them on rocks and logs to mark territory, and the flat sides stop them rolling off.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine: Why wombats make cube-shaped poos

setup: To work out why wombats produce cube-shaped droppings, researchers studied the guts of wombats killed by cars by...
answer: inflating a long balloon inside their intestines
detail: Stretching the gut showed some parts were far stretchier than others. The cubes take shape in the final 8% of the intestine, where the uneven walls press out corners.
source_title: Physics World: Why wombats have cube-shaped poo

setup: A Venus flytrap snaps shut after its trigger hairs are touched twice, but it only starts releasing digestive juices once they have been touched...
detail: A 2016 study showed the plant effectively counts. The second touch must come within about 20 seconds of the first to spring the trap; five or more switch on its digestive glands.
source_title: Discover Magazine: Venus flytraps count to 5 before dissolving prey

setup: When mallard ducks sleep in a row, the birds at each end tend to keep one eye open, usually the eye...
detail: Niels Rattenborg found end ducks kept their outward eye open 86% of the time, with the matching half of the brain awake. Ducks in the middle could shut both eyes.
source_title: University of Alaska Fairbanks: Bird brains stay alert while ducks sleep

setup: During El Niño famines in the Galápagos, marine iguanas survive the food shortage by...
answer: shrinking in length by up to 20 percent
detail: Scientists found the iguanas actually get shorter, some by almost 7cm, then grow back when food returns. The biggest iguanas shrank the most and survived longest.
source_title: Science News: Famine reveals incredible shrinking iguanas

setup: The hoatzin, a South American bird, is known locally as the 'stinkbird' because it smells of...
detail: It eats leaves and ferments them in a hugely enlarged crop, much as a cow does in its stomach, burping methane as it goes. It's the only bird known to digest its food this way.
source_title: World Land Trust: Meet the Amazon's smelliest bird

setup: Hoatzin chicks can't fly for their first couple of months, so they climb around the treetops using...
detail: The claws help the chicks clamber through branches and escape predators. A 2015 genetic study suggested the bird is the last of a lineage that split off around 64 million years ago.
source_title: World Land Trust: Meet the Amazon's smelliest bird

setup: When a predator chases a young hoatzin out of its nest above a river, the chick escapes by...
answer: jumping into the water and swimming away
detail: Hoatzins build their nests over water. Chased chicks drop in, swim underwater, and later climb back up to the nest using the claws on their wings.

setup: Before going to sleep each night, some parrotfish protect themselves from blood-sucking parasites by...
answer: wrapping themselves in a sleeping bag of mucus
detail: The fish puff out the snot cocoon around themselves every evening. In a lab test, around 95% of uncovered fish were attacked by parasites, compared with about 10% of those in cocoons.
source_title: Live Science: Mucus cocoons protect fish from parasites

setup: In 2010 Japanese scientists placed oat flakes in the positions of cities around Tokyo and let a slime mould grow between them. The slime mould...
detail: Atsushi Tero's team let the brainless mould spread from the centre. The network of tubes it formed to link the food sources closely resembled the real railway system.
source_title: ScienceDaily: Slime mould mimics Tokyo rail network

setup: A common mushroom called the split gill fungus doesn't have just two sexes. It has more than...
detail: Its mating types are set by many variants at four genetic spots, and the combinations add up to over 23,000. That lets it mate with the vast majority of other split gills it meets.
source_title: Popular Science: This fungus has over 23,000 sexes

setup: In 2012 researchers at Queen Mary University of London found that young goats raised together...
detail: Pygmy goat kids were recorded at one week and five weeks old. Kids in the same social group came to sound more alike as they grew, showing their calls are shaped by their companions.
source_title: Queen Mary University of London: Goat kids develop accents

setup: Lobsters communicate with each other by...
answer: squirting urine out of their faces
detail: Their urine comes from nephropores at the base of the large antennae and is packed with chemical signals. Lobsters squirt it at rivals during fights and at potential mates.
source_title: Snopes: Lobsters 'pee' out of their faces

setup: A female lobster hoping to move in with a dominant male calms his aggression by...
detail: Her urine contains pheromones signalling she's ready to mate and reduces his aggression. If accepted she can stay in his burrow for up to two weeks.
source_title: Snopes: Lobsters 'pee' out of their faces

setup: To prove that dung beetles steer by looking at the night sky, researchers fitted some of them with...
detail: The caps blocked the beetles' view of the sky, and those wearing them took far longer to roll their dung balls away, wandering instead of heading straight. The study was published in Current Biology.
source_title: National Geographic: Dung beetles use the Milky Way to navigate

setup: The tongue-eating louse is a parasite that cuts off the blood supply to a fish's tongue until it drops off, and then...
detail: Cymothoa exigua clings to the stub of the old tongue, and the fish can use it like a prosthetic organ.

setup: A diner in south London preparing a red snapper for lunch got a shock when they found...
answer: a tongue-eating parasite in its mouth
detail: The Horniman Museum identified it as a tongue-eating louse. Its natural history keeper said he hadn't seen one in all his 13 years at the museum.
source_title: Practical Fishkeeping: Tongue-eating louse found on supermarket snapper

setup: When a snapping shrimp clicks its claw, the collapsing bubble it creates is so violent that it...
answer: gives off a flash of light
detail: A 2001 paper in Nature dubbed the effect 'shrimpoluminescence'. The bubble's implosion creates extreme pressure and temperatures, as well as the loud snap.
source_title: University of Twente: Sound (and light) of the snapping shrimp

setup: Greenland sharks can live for up to around 400 years, and they don't reach adulthood until they are about...
detail: A 2016 study dated the sharks using the centres of their eye lenses, which form before birth. It made them the longest-lived vertebrates known.

setup: Scientists worked out the age of Greenland sharks using radioactive traces left in their eyes by...
detail: Bomb tests spiked carbon-14 levels worldwide. Comparing the levels in the sharks' eye lenses suggested the largest studied was roughly 392 years old. They grow less than an inch a year.
source_title: The Local Denmark: Greenland sharks may live 400 years

setup: Glass frogs turn almost see-through while they sleep by hiding up to 89% of their red blood cells in...
detail: A 2022 study found the frogs pack their red blood cells into the liver while resting. When awake, the blood returns to circulation and they look reddish-brown.
source_title: Phys.org: Scientists reveal secrets of frog transparency

setup: In 2021 Japanese scientists found sea slugs that can cut off their own heads and then...
detail: Researchers think the severed head survives by photosynthesising, a trick these slugs pick up from algae they eat. One slug lost and regrew its body twice.
source_title: CBC News: Sea slugs regrow bodies after decapitation

setup: A 2022 study at Queen Mary University of London found that bumblebees will happily spend time...
answer: rolling little balls around for fun
detail: The bees repeatedly rolled wooden balls with no food reward, and younger bees seemed more playful than older ones. Researchers said it was evidence of play in insects.

setup: When a toad swallows a bombardier beetle, the beetle can escape by...
answer: spraying hot chemicals until the toad vomits it up
detail: In Kobe University experiments, 43% of beetles that could spray were brought back up alive, one after 107 minutes inside the toad. Nearly all beetles without their spray were digested.
source_title: National Geographic: Beetle survives being eaten by toad

setup: To stop themselves drifting off while sleeping on the sea, sea otters often...
detail: Otters sleep in groups called rafts, usually of about 50 animals, kept together by touching or anchoring in kelp. The famous hand-holding happens but is actually quite rare in the wild.
source_title: Discover Magazine: Do sea otters hold hands while sleeping?

setup: A University of Washington study found that if crows see a masked person holding a dead crow, they will...
answer: scold that person for weeks afterwards
detail: In Kaeli Swift's experiments, the crows kept scolding the masked volunteers when they came back empty-handed over the next six weeks, and stayed wary of the spot for days.

setup: Australian health authorities say the best first aid for a sting from the Gympie-gympie tree is to use...
detail: The tiny stinging hairs carry a neurotoxin, and pain can last from days to months. Wax strips pull the hairs out; scratching or rubbing breaks them and makes it worse.

setup: Scientists studying the toxins of Australia's ferocious Gympie-gympie stinging tree discovered they closely resemble...
detail: The pain-causing molecules, named gympietides, fold into shapes like spider and cone snail toxins and hit the same pain receptors. The pain can last for days or weeks.
source_title: The Science Breaker: Australia's giant stinging tree

setup: Rafflesia arnoldii produces flowers up to a metre across, yet the plant itself has...
detail: It is a parasite that lives almost unseen inside a vine of the grape family, only emerging to flower. The bloom smells of rotting meat to attract carrion flies.
source_title: Kew Plants of the World Online: Rafflesia arnoldii

setup: Unlike most flowers, which make powdery pollen, the giant Rafflesia flower produces its pollen as...
answer: a sticky fluid a bit like snot
detail: The gooey pollen dries on visiting carrion flies and may stay viable for weeks. The flower also warms itself up, which helps spread its rotten-meat smell.
source_title: ZME Science: The corpse flower that steals genes

setup: In Oregon's Malheur National Forest there is a single honey fungus that covers more than three square miles and may be...
detail: Nicknamed the Humongous Fungus, it grows mostly underground, spreading roughly one to three feet a year and killing trees by rotting their roots as it goes.
source_title: OPB Oregon Field Guide: Humongous fungus

setup: Darwin's bark spider of Madagascar builds giant webs over rivers and lakes, using single bridge lines that can stretch...
answer: more than 10 metres across the water
detail: Its silk is more than twice as tough as any previously described spider silk, and over ten times tougher than Kevlar.

setup: When scientists decoded nearly 15,000 calls made by Egyptian fruit bats, they found most of them were...
detail: The bats were mostly bickering over food, arguing about sleeping spots, and protesting against unwanted mating attempts.
source_title: NPR: When bats squeak, they tend to squabble

setup: Vampire bats that have had a good night's hunting will help hungry roost-mates by...
answer: throwing up blood into their mouths
detail: A vampire bat that misses three nights of feeding can starve. Gerald Carter's studies found that unfamiliar bats groom each other first, building trust before they start sharing blood.

setup: When threatened by a coyote or fox, a horned lizard can defend itself by...
detail: It raises the blood pressure in its head until vessels around the eyes burst, firing blood up to 1.5 metres. Dogs and their wild relatives find it foul-tasting; birds aren't put off.

setup: Hippos ooze a blood-red liquid from their skin that works as...
detail: Nicknamed 'blood sweat', it is neither blood nor sweat. Its red and orange pigments absorb ultraviolet light, and the red one also slows the growth of harmful bacteria.
source_title: Mongabay: Hippo sweat could serve as sunscreen

setup: Hippos mark their territory by going to the toilet while...
answer: flicking their tails to spray the dung about
detail: The tail swishes back and forth like a fan, sending dung flying over the surrounding area. The National Wildlife Federation describes it as a key part of how hippos mark their patch.
source_title: National Wildlife Federation: In Heaven With Hippos

setup: In 2021 Russian scientists revived microscopic animals called bdelloid rotifers that had been frozen in Siberian permafrost for...
detail: Radiocarbon dating confirmed their age. Once thawed, the rotifers carried on reproducing by cloning themselves, without any need for a mate.
source_title: Smithsonian Magazine: Scientists revive tiny animals after 24,000 years

setup: In 2007 the European Space Agency sent around 3,000 tiny water bears into orbit and exposed them to...
detail: The tardigrades spent 12 days on the Foton-M3 mission. The experiment leader said the vacuum and cosmic radiation 'were not a problem for water bears'.
source_title: European Space Agency: Tiny animals survive exposure to space

setup: Australia's mistletoebird helps spread mistletoe by eating its berries and then planting the sticky seeds on branches by...
detail: The bird has no muscular gizzard, so berries pass through very quickly and seeds come out intact. It then rubs them onto branches where they can sprout.
source_title: BBC Wildlife: Weirdest animals in Australia

setup: Australia's thorny devil lizard can drink from damp sand just by touching it, because tiny channels between its scales make the water...
detail: The desert reptile shovels damp sand onto its back, and capillary action in the grooves between its scales wicks the moisture to its mouth.
source_title: BBC Wildlife: Weirdest animals in Australia

setup: To confuse predators, the thorny devil lizard has a lump on the back of its neck that acts as...
detail: The spiny desert reptile's false head is designed to mislead predators about where its real head is. It lives in the Australian desert.
source_title: BBC Wildlife: Weirdest animals in Australia

setup: The numbat, an endangered marsupial from Western Australia, eats almost nothing but termites, getting through as many as...
detail: It eats between 15,000 and 20,000 termites daily, catching them with a very long tongue. Its range has shrunk to a few small colonies.
source_title: BBC Wildlife: Weirdest animals in Australia

setup: Central Africa's hairy frog defends itself Wolverine-style: when threatened, it breaks the bones in its own toes so that...
answer: the sharp ends pierce its skin as claws
detail: It flexes a muscle to snap the bone tip free and drive it out through the skin. Afterwards the bones are pulled back and the skin heals.

setup: Lizards can drop their tails to escape a predator, but when some sea cucumbers are threatened, they instead...
answer: shoot out their internal organs and regrow them
detail: Depending on the species, the guts come out through the mouth end or the rear. The sea cucumber regrows them within a few weeks.
source_title: The Conversation: Amazing animal defence mechanisms

setup: A platypus finds its prey using its bill, which contains more than 40,000...
detail: The electroreceptors pick up tiny electrical fields from the muscles of shrimp and worms. The platypus is one of only five living egg-laying mammals.
source_title: BBC Wildlife: Weirdest animals in Australia

setup: In 1841, the technique still used to pollinate almost all the world's vanilla was worked out on the island of Réunion by...
answer: a 12-year-old enslaved boy called Edmond Albius
detail: Albius found he could lift a tiny flap inside the flower and press the pollen on by hand. Before that, vanilla only fruited reliably in Mexico, where local insects did the job.

setup: A vanilla orchid flower stays open for only about one day, so a farmer who wants a pod has to pollinate it by hand within...
detail: Partly because of this labour, vanilla is the second most expensive spice by weight, after saffron. Growers walk their vines daily to catch each flower.

setup: Castoreum, which the US Food and Drug Administration regards as safe to use as a 'natural flavouring' for vanilla and raspberry, comes from...
answer: scent glands near a beaver's bottom
detail: Beavers use it to mark territory. It is very rarely used in food now: in 1987 the US got through only about 250 pounds a year, and less since.

setup: Fanta was invented in Nazi Germany when Coca-Cola syrup couldn't be imported. The original recipe was made from beet sugar, apple pulp and...
answer: whey, left over from making cheese
detail: Max Keith, head of Coca-Cola in Germany, called the ingredients 'the leftovers of leftovers'. The name came from the German word Fantasie.

setup: During the Second World War, sugar was so tightly rationed in Germany that many bottles of Fanta were used...
detail: Three million cases were sold in Germany in 1943. Many of those bottles were cooked with rather than drunk.

setup: The orange Fanta we know today wasn't German at all. It was first made in 1955 in...
detail: The wartime German Fanta was dropped as a brand in 1949. Coca-Cola relaunched it as Fanta Orange in Italy in 1955.

setup: When Fred Baur, the designer of the Pringles tube, died in 2008, part of his ashes were buried in a Pringles can, after his children briefly debated...
detail: His son Larry insisted on Original. They picked up the can at a Walgreens on the way to the funeral home.

setup: In 2008, Procter & Gamble briefly convinced a British court that Pringles weren't crisps, partly by arguing that their shape...
detail: They were trying to avoid VAT on crisps. The Court of Appeal overturned the ruling in 2009, finding they had more than enough potato.

setup: Pringles' moustached mascot is now officially called Julius Pringles, a name the company only accepted in 2013 after it first appeared...
answer: as a prank edit on Wikipedia
detail: In 2006 a student, Justin Shillock, added the made-up name, citing a parody wiki as his source. Before that the mascot was simply 'Mr P'.

setup: When Twinkies were invented in 1930, their cream filling was flavoured with...
detail: The switch to vanilla came in the Second World War, when bananas were rationed. Vanilla proved so popular that it stayed.

setup: Twinkies were invented because a bakery manager wanted to use the pans for strawberry shortcakes, which otherwise sat idle...
answer: for all but six weeks of the year
detail: James Dewar of the Continental Baking Company filled small sponge cakes with banana cream so the equipment earned its keep.

setup: James Dewar said he got the name 'Twinkie' from a billboard in St Louis advertising...
detail: Dewar was a manager at the Continental Baking Company, which later became Hostess.

setup: Caesar salad is generally credited to Caesar Cardini, an Italian immigrant, who is said to have created it in 1924 in...
detail: Cardini lived in San Diego but ran his restaurant over the border so American customers could drink alcohol during Prohibition.

setup: Julia Child recalled that the Caesar salad she ate in the 1920s was meant to be eaten...
answer: with your fingers, as whole lettuce leaves
detail: Cardini's daughter said the original had no anchovies; the fishy taste came from Worcestershire sauce. It was tossed at the table for show.
source_title: Country & Town House: Caesar salad history

setup: The main ingredient of bird's nest soup, one of the most expensive foods in the world, is a nest built almost entirely out of...
detail: Swiftlets build cup-shaped nests from layers of saliva, which sets hard in air. Top grades can sell for thousands of dollars a kilo.

setup: In Indonesia and Malaysia, edible swiftlet nests are 'farmed' in empty buildings, with the birds lured in by...
detail: Speakers hang in the windows of these 'house farms'. Malaysia had about 60,000 swiftlet houses by 2013, up from 900 in 1998.

setup: Until 2017, Guinness wasn't suitable for vegans because the beer was cleared using...
answer: a substance made from dried fish bladders
detail: The fining agent, isinglass, was dropped after Guinness built a new filtration system at St James's Gate. Draught went first, cans and bottles later.

setup: In 1991, McVitie's fought a tax tribunal to prove Jaffa Cakes were cakes, not biscuits. To help win, they brought to court...
detail: Chocolate-covered biscuits attract VAT but cakes don't. McVitie's won, so Jaffa Cakes are still VAT-free.

setup: A key argument in the 1991 Jaffa Cake VAT case was what happens when one is left out: unlike a stale biscuit, a stale Jaffa Cake...
answer: goes hard, just like a cake
detail: Biscuits go soft when stale. The tribunal decided Jaffa Cakes had enough of the characteristics of cakes, so they stay VAT-free.

setup: Supermarkets are allowed to sell their own 'Jaffa Cakes' because McVitie's...
detail: McVitie & Price launched them in 1927. Because the name was never protected, many rival brands use it.

setup: In 1835, John Cook Bennett became president of a medical college in Ohio, and chose to give his very first lecture on...
detail: Bennett claimed tomatoes could treat diarrhoea, indigestion and even cholera. He was also known for selling medical degrees for $10.

setup: The word 'ketchup' probably comes from a word in the Hokkien Chinese dialect meaning...
detail: Early British ketchups contained no tomato. Mushrooms, walnuts and oysters were all used.

setup: Long before tomato ketchup took over, the ketchup splashed on meat and fish in Georgian and Victorian Britain was made from...
detail: Salted mushrooms gave up their juice, which was boiled with spices such as mace and nutmeg, then strained. Americans later sweetened tomato versions.

setup: In 2022, Oxford scientists worked out how to stop a nearly empty ketchup bottle from splattering: squeeze more slowly and...
answer: use a bottle with a wider nozzle
detail: Air in the bottle compresses like a spring and, once the sauce runs low, bursts out with the last of it. Taking the cap off near the end also helps.

setup: According to company legend, Lea & Perrins' first batch of Worcestershire sauce tasted awful, so the barrel was left in a cellar. It became edible after...
detail: When the chemists tried it again, it had mellowed. The first bottles went on sale in 1838.

setup: Lea & Perrins claimed its recipe came from Lord Sandys, a former Governor of Bengal. The problem is that...
answer: no Lord Sandys was ever Governor of Bengal
detail: Records show no Baron Sandys held that role or even visited India. The original label just said 'a nobleman in the county'.

setup: In Brazil, Portugal and Mexico, Worcestershire sauce isn't named after Worcester. It's simply called...
detail: It's 'molho inglês' in Portuguese and 'salsa inglesa' in Spanish. In Japan the bottles just say 'Worcester'.

setup: When Atlanta banned alcohol in 1886, John Pemberton reworked his wine-based tonic and advertised the new Coca-Cola as...
detail: His earlier product was Pemberton's French Wine Coca. He also claimed Coca-Cola could cure impotence and morphine addiction.

setup: When Coca-Cola commissioned its famous contour bottle, the brief asked for a shape you could recognise by touch in the dark, and even...
answer: when it was smashed on the ground
detail: Designer Earl R. Dean couldn't find a picture of coca or kola, so he based the ridged shape on a cocoa pod he saw in an encyclopedia. The bottle was patented in 1915.

setup: Before Coca-Cola settled on its Chinese name, shopkeepers made up their own versions that sounded right but meant things like...
detail: Another meant 'female horse fastened with wax'. The company registered its own Chinese name in 1928, which means roughly 'allow the mouth to rejoice'.

setup: Welsh harpist Nansi Richards claimed she gave Kellogg's the idea for its cockerel mascot, because the Welsh word for cockerel, 'ceiliog', sounds like...
detail: She was a friend of the Kellogg family. The surname Kellogg has no actual link to the Welsh word.

setup: The Kellogg brothers fell out badly in 1906 when Will Kellogg decided to add something to cornflakes that his brother John disapproved of...
detail: John wanted a plain diet for patients at his health sanitarium. Will founded his own company to sell the sweetened version.

setup: At his health sanitarium, John Harvey Kellogg had patients take a pint of yoghurt, half of it eaten and the other half...
detail: The idea was to plant 'protective germs where they are most needed'. Patients included Thomas Edison and Amelia Earhart.

setup: The first known recipe for potato crisps didn't come from America. It appeared in 1817 in...
answer: a London cookbook called The Cook's Oracle
detail: William Kitchiner's recipe was for 'potatoes fried in slices or shavings'. The famous Saratoga Springs story came decades later.

setup: In the legend of how crisps were invented, the fussy customer is the tycoon Cornelius Vanderbilt. But he was only written into the story in 1973 by...
detail: St Regis Paper made crisp packets. Vanderbilt was touring Europe at the time of the supposed 1853 incident, and historians consider the George Crum story a myth.

setup: In the 14th century, a war lasting fourteen weeks broke out after a group of noblemen stole a shipment of...
detail: Saffron was in huge demand for medicines during the Black Death, making a stolen cargo worth fighting over.

setup: In medieval Nuremberg, anyone caught selling saffron that had been bulked out with cheaper stuff could be...
detail: The city's Safranschou code dealt harshly with fakes. Around 150,000 crocus flowers are needed for one kilo of saffron.

setup: Saffron recovered from a Danish-Norwegian warship that sank in the Baltic Sea more than 500 years ago still...
detail: The spice was found aboard the wreck of the flagship Gribshunden, still with its distinctive aroma.

setup: In Nelson's navy, sailors were sometimes served 'Scotch coffee' for breakfast, which was actually...
answer: burnt bread boiled in water and sweetened with sugar
detail: A Trafalgar veteran described it in his memoirs. The other breakfast option was burgoo, a porridge of coarse oatmeal and water.

setup: The invention of instant coffee is credited to a coffee merchant who patented a soluble coffee powder in 1890 in...
detail: David Strang made his 'Soluble Dry Coffee-powder' by blowing hot air over liquid coffee. His role was largely forgotten until the 2000s.

setup: One of the world's most expensive coffees, Black Ivory, is made in Thailand from beans that have been...
detail: It sells for up to $1,100 a kilo. The better-known kopi luwak goes through a civet instead.

setup: In 1901, Victorian cookery writer Agnes Marshall suggested dinner guests could freeze their ice cream instantly at the table using...
detail: She wrote about it in her magazine The Table, saying 'as a table adjunct its powers are astonishing'. Liquid nitrogen ice cream is now a novelty dessert.

setup: Merchant records show that in the summer of 1790, George Washington spent about $200 on...
detail: That was a large sum at the time. Thomas Jefferson, meanwhile, left an 18-step recipe for making ice cream.

setup: The earliest known use of the word 'pizza' is in a Latin document from 997 AD, which says a tenant owed the local bishop...
answer: twelve pizzas every Christmas and Easter
detail: The document comes from Gaeta in Italy, then part of the Byzantine Empire. The Christmas payment also included a pork shoulder and a kidney.

setup: France's hated salt tax, the gabelle, helped spark the French Revolution and wasn't finally abolished until...
detail: It was scrapped in 1790, but Napoleon brought it back to pay for his wars. It lasted until just after the Second World War.

setup: Herodotus and Aristotle both wrote that cinnamon was gathered by...
answer: knocking down the nests of giant birds that built with it
detail: Aristotle said locals shot down the nests with lead-weighted arrows. Pliny the Elder dismissed it as a tale invented by traders to justify high prices.

setup: In 18th-century Britain, pineapples were such status symbols that at dinner parties they were often...
answer: displayed rather than eaten, and reused until they rotted
detail: Growing them in hothouses cost a fortune. The Earl of Dunmore even topped his hothouse with a 14-metre stone pineapple.

setup: One theory says mayonnaise is named after Mahón in Menorca, where the French are said to have found the sauce after...
detail: The Duke of Richelieu's forces seized the port. Similar garlic-and-oil sauces existed in Catalonia centuries earlier.

setup: Carmine, the red food colouring labelled E120, is made from...
answer: crushed insects, about 70,000 per pound of dye
detail: The insects are called cochineal. Carmine colours sweets, drinks, sausages and some cheeses.

setup: At the 1893 Chicago World's Fair, a giant Canadian cheese weighing 22,000 pounds...
answer: fell through the floor, but still won a bronze medal
detail: The 'mammoth cheese' came from Perth, Ontario. It was moved to a reinforced concrete floor and went on to win an award.

setup: The word 'spud' for a potato originally meant...
detail: The word dates from the 15th century. Potatoes were only called spuds from the 1840s.

setup: The Danish astronomer Tycho Brahe lost part of his nose in a duel. When scientists dug him up in 2010, traces on his skull showed his false nose was made of...
answer: brass, not the gold or silver of legend
detail: Copper and zinc found in the bone around his nose pointed to a brass prosthesis. For centuries it had been described as gold and silver.
source_title: Scientific American: Tycho Brahe not poisoned after all

setup: Tycho Brahe owned a tame elk. While it was staying at a nobleman's castle, it died after it...
answer: got drunk on beer and fell down the stairs
detail: His biographer Pierre Gassendi recorded that the elk climbed the castle stairs, drank a large amount of beer and tumbled to its death.
source_title: Mental Floss: Tycho Brahe's drunken moose

setup: Tycho Brahe's final illness in 1601 began at a banquet in Prague, where he was too polite to...
answer: leave the table to go to the toilet
detail: He drank heavily and would not excuse himself. Afterwards he could not urinate, and he died about eleven days later.

setup: Tycho Brahe kept a jester called Jepp, who was said to have psychic powers. During meals, Jepp sat...
detail: Jepp was a dwarf whom Brahe believed to be clairvoyant. He reportedly sat beneath the table while Brahe and his guests ate.
source_title: Mental Floss: Tycho Brahe's suspicious death

setup: Tycho Brahe is said to have carried a small pot with him wherever he went. It contained...
answer: putty for sticking his metal nose back on
detail: Accounts describe him reattaching his prosthetic nose with an adhesive he kept with him whenever it came loose.
source_title: ENT & Audiology News: The astronomer's nose

setup: When his son complained about a disgusting new tax, Emperor Vespasian held some of the takings under his nose and asked if they smelt. The tax was on...
detail: Urine was sold to tanners and launderers for its ammonia. Vespasian's retort is the origin of the saying 'pecunia non olet': money doesn't stink.
source_title: HeritageDaily: The Roman tax on urine

setup: In 19th-century Paris, public street urinals were given a name honouring...
detail: The Prefect Rambuteau suggested 'vespasiennes' after the emperor who taxed urine. Italians still call urinals 'vespasiani'.

setup: Before he became emperor, Vespasian went into business to fix his finances, earning the nickname...
answer: the muleteer, because he traded in mules
detail: Roman sources record the nickname 'mulio' after he entered the mule trade following his governorship in Africa.

setup: The future emperor Vespasian fell out of favour with Nero after he...
answer: nodded off while Nero was singing
detail: Suetonius says he often left the theatre during Nero's performances and fell asleep if he stayed. He was kept away from power for a time afterwards.

setup: According to Suetonius, while Vespasian was governing a Roman province in Africa, the locals once pelted him with...
detail: It happened during a riot at the town of Hadrumetum. Apart from that, Suetonius says he governed the province with great integrity.

setup: When the young Vespasian did a poor job of keeping Rome's streets clean, Emperor Caligula punished him by...
answer: having soldiers stuff muck down his toga
detail: Vespasian held a minor post responsible for street cleaning. Caligula had soldiers fill the fold of his toga with filth from the streets.

setup: When Emperor Vespasian fell fatally ill in AD 79, he joked...
answer: 'Dear me, I think I'm becoming a god'
detail: Roman emperors were declared gods after death, so he was mocking the custom. Suetonius says he also insisted an emperor should die standing.

setup: At the Olympic Games of AD 67, Emperor Nero was thrown from his ten-horse chariot and never finished the race. The judges...
detail: Suetonius records that he was crowned regardless. After Nero's death his wins were struck off the list of Olympic victors.

setup: At the opening games of the Colosseum in AD 80, Emperor Titus had spectators showered with...
answer: wooden balls that could be swapped for prizes
detail: The balls could be exchanged for clothing, gold and other goods. The opening games lasted a hundred days.

setup: According to the Talmud, Emperor Titus was punished for destroying the Temple in Jerusalem by...
answer: a gnat that lived in his brain for seven years
detail: The legend says the insect flew up his nose and gnawed at his brain. Later Jewish scholars read the tale as an allegory.

setup: The English surnames Fuller, Tucker and Walker all come from the same old trade, which involved...
answer: thickening woollen cloth, often by trampling it in stale urine
detail: Fulling was also called 'walking' or 'tucking'. Stale urine, known as 'lant', supplied ammonia that cleaned the wool.

setup: Pope Boniface VI, elected amid riots in Rome in April 896, held the job for just...
detail: He reigned from 11 to 26 April 896. He had twice been stripped of his clerical orders before becoming pope.

setup: In 882 Pope John VIII was murdered by his own clergy, who first poisoned him and then...
detail: Possible motives include an empty papal treasury and his failure to stop Saracen raids.

setup: Returning from Western Europe in 1698, Peter the Great made his point at a reception in his honour by...
answer: shaving his guests' beards himself with a barber's razor
detail: His victims were leading nobles and officials. Long beards were a mark of Orthodox piety in Russia, so it caused outrage.
source_title: Smithsonian: Peter the Great's beard tax

setup: In 1386 the town of Falaise hanged a sow for killing a baby. The executioner's surviving bill includes extra money for...
detail: The receipt pays him ten sous and ten deniers, plus ten sous for a new glove. It is the only primary source for the case.
source_title: Executed Today: The Sow of Falaise

setup: In 1457 a sow in Burgundy was convicted of killing a child. Her six piglets were tried too, but...
detail: The piglets were found at the scene but no one could prove they took part. Their mother was hanged.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: When societies put animals on trial

setup: In 1522 the rats of Autun were summoned to court for eating barley. Their lawyer said they couldn't safely attend because...
answer: the town was full of cats
detail: Defence lawyer Bartholomew Chassenée argued that a defendant may ignore a summons if attending is dangerous. The case collapsed.

setup: In 1713, Franciscan friars in Brazil took termites to court for eating their monastery. The tribunal ordered the friars to...
answer: give the termites their own patch of land
detail: The termites' lawyer argued they were God's creatures entitled to food. The termites were ordered to stay in the new home.

setup: In 1519 a judge in the Alpine village of Stelvio banished the local moles, but guaranteed them...
answer: safe passage, protected from cats and dogs
detail: Pregnant moles and newborns were given extra time to leave town.

setup: In Basel in 1474, a cockerel was sentenced to death for the crime of...
detail: People feared an egg from a cockerel would hatch a basilisk, a monster that could kill with a look.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: When societies put animals on trial

setup: In 1379 a herd of pigs in eastern France was accused of killing a swineherd's son. Some were saved when the Duke of Burgundy...
answer: issued the pigs a formal pardon
detail: The pigs belonged partly to a local abbey, which wrote to Duke Philip the Bold insisting its pigs were well-behaved and innocent.

setup: One 15th-century French pig accused of killing a person spent...
answer: five years in jail before being executed
detail: Officials even had to ask Duke John the Fearless for permission to build a gallows for it.

setup: When flies prosecuted in 15th-century Mainz failed to turn up to court, the judges...
answer: appointed them a better defence lawyer
detail: Medieval courts took animal defendants' rights seriously, including the right to proper legal counsel.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: When societies put animals on trial

setup: Trinity College, Cambridge banned students from keeping dogs, so the young Lord Byron kept...
detail: He may have bought it at Stourbridge Fair. The rules mentioned dogs but said nothing about bears.

setup: After university, Byron's pet bear moved to Newstead Abbey, where it roamed the grounds alongside...
detail: Byron also kept a fox, a crocodile, a honey badger, geese and a goat with a broken leg at various homes.

setup: Visiting Byron in Ravenna in 1821, Percy Shelley found the house full of animals, including, on the staircase...
answer: five peacocks, two guinea hens and an Egyptian crane
detail: Shelley also counted ten horses, eight large dogs, three monkeys, five cats, an eagle, a crow and a falcon.

setup: Byron claimed his Cambridge bear inspired Thomas Love Peacock's satirical novel 'Melincourt', whose hero is an orangutan who...
answer: is made a baronet and elected to Parliament
detail: Sir Oran Haut-ton becomes MP for the borough of 'One Vote', mocking rotten boroughs.

setup: In 1847 the Oxford geologist William Buckland brought his pet bear to a scientific gathering, dressed in...
detail: The bear, Tiglath Pileser, was later banished from Christ Church, scared a sweetshop owner in Islip and ended up at the zoo.

setup: Mary Toft's 1726 rabbit-birth hoax finally fell apart in London when...
answer: a porter was caught smuggling a rabbit into her room
detail: He admitted her sister-in-law had asked him for the smallest rabbit he could find. Mary confessed soon after.

setup: When Mary Toft, the woman who 'gave birth to rabbits', died in 1763, the parish register recorded her as...
detail: She had spent four months in Bridewell prison, where crowds came to gawp at her, before being released without charge.

setup: John Howard, the surgeon who first attended Mary Toft's 'rabbit births', kept the rabbits she 'delivered'...
answer: pickled in jars on a shelf in his study
detail: Howard had alerted the King's court to the case. The hoax badly damaged the reputations of several leading doctors.

setup: During the 1726 scandal over a woman who claimed to give birth to rabbits, Londoners reportedly stopped...
answer: eating rabbit stew and jugged hare
detail: The idea of rabbits growing inside a woman put people off the dish while the case was in the news.

setup: After her rabbit hoax was exposed, Mary Toft was sometimes shown off by the Duke of Richmond as...
answer: a curiosity at his dinner parties
detail: The Duke displayed her at his house in Godalming. Hogarth also mocked the whole affair in prints.

setup: An 18th-century myth claimed Dutch women could give birth to a mole-like creature called a 'sooterkin' because they...
answer: kept warm by sitting on stoves
detail: The warmth was supposed to breed the creature inside them. Some eminent physicians of the day believed it.

setup: In spring 1830 Paris installed its first public urinals on the boulevards. By July most had been destroyed because they were...
answer: used to build barricades in the revolution
detail: The prefect Rambuteau later installed more than 400 masonry urinals, nicknamed 'Rambuteau columns'.

setup: The recipe instruction 'First catch your hare' is famously credited to the cook Hannah Glasse, but her book actually says...
detail: The misquote became popular in the 19th century. To 'case' an animal meant to take its skin off. Her 18th-century book 'The Art of Cookery' includes jugged hare.

setup: Henry VIII's planned tomb reused parts of Cardinal Wolsey's. Its sarcophagus was finally used centuries later for...
detail: It now sits in the crypt of St Paul's Cathedral. Henry himself lies at St George's Chapel, Windsor.

setup: After Charles I was beheaded in 1649, he was buried at Windsor in the same vault as...
detail: He was laid to rest at St George's Chapel more than a century after Henry's death.

setup: When his first wife, Catherine of Aragon, died in January 1536, Henry VIII reportedly marked the occasion by...
detail: He was said to wear yellow with a white feather in his cap. By then he was already married to Anne Boleyn.

setup: By the 1750s a Soho grocer was selling 'Sir Hans Sloane's Milk Chocolate' as...
detail: Sloane, the physician whose collection founded the British Museum, probably came across chocolate mixed with milk in Jamaica.

setup: After his marriage to Sophia Dorothea broke down, the future King George I...
answer: locked her up in a German castle for over 30 years
detail: She was confined at Ahlden House in Celle until her death. She never became queen of Great Britain.

setup: 'Voltaire' was itself a pen name. During his lifetime, the writer used at least...
detail: He was born François-Marie Arouet and was jailed twice in the Bastille for his writing and his feuds.

setup: Voltaire made a fortune that set him up for life by...
answer: joining a syndicate that bought up a government lottery
detail: The mathematician La Condamine proposed the scheme over dinner. Voltaire may have made a million livres and invested it shrewdly.

setup: In 1812 General Claude-François de Malet tried to seize power in Paris using...
answer: a forged announcement that Napoleon was dead
detail: The coup failed and Malet was shot with his fellow plotters. When the volley left him only wounded, he reportedly shouted 'You forgot me!'

setup: At his murder trial in the Cherokee Nation, Archilla Smith passed the time by...
answer: lending his pipe to the judge and jury
detail: An eyewitness said the judge and jurors kept wandering over to borrow it. He was hanged on 1 January 1841 from a tree branch, because the gallows had not arrived.

setup: In 1817, a Warwickshire man acquitted of murder was hauled back to court by the victim's brother. He escaped a second trial by demanding...
answer: trial by battle against the brother
detail: Abraham Thornton invoked an ancient right that had never been repealed. William Ashford declined to fight, Thornton walked free in 1818, and Parliament abolished trial by battle in 1819.

setup: In 1336, a drunken sailor fell to his death on a ship moored in the Thames. Under English law, the coroner's jury confiscated...
answer: the rope, valued at ten shillings
detail: Under the law of 'deodands', any object that caused a death was forfeited to the Crown for pious use. Ten shillings was roughly the price of a good horse.

setup: On Christmas Eve 1841, a train hit a landslip at Sonning Cutting, killing eight passengers outright. Using a medieval law, the inquest jury declared that...
answer: the engine and carriages must forfeit £1,000
detail: Juries used 'deodands' (objects that caused a death) to punish railway firms. The award was overturned on appeal, and deodands were abolished in 1846.

setup: Medieval English law confiscated whatever object caused a death. When someone was fatally scalded, one jury decided the guilty object was...
answer: the pot, not the boiling water
detail: Deodands could be almost anything movable: horses, carts, haystacks, beer vats, boats and trees all qualified. Owners usually paid the item's value rather than hand it over.

setup: For centuries, English convicts who could read a verse from Psalm 51 could avoid hanging. As a result, the passage got the nickname...
detail: Reading it proved you were 'clergy', moving your case to the more lenient church courts. Illiterate criminals simply memorised it. The literacy test was scrapped in 1706.
source_title: Academic Kids Encyclopedia: Benefit of clergy

setup: Under Henry VII, non-clergy who dodged the gallows by reading a Bible verse could only do it once, because they were...
detail: The brand marked them as having used 'benefit of clergy', disqualifying a second claim. Branding was abolished in 1779 and the benefit itself in 1827.
source_title: Academic Kids Encyclopedia: Benefit of clergy

setup: From 1547, English peers could claim 'benefit of clergy' to escape the death penalty even if they...
answer: couldn't read, and more than once
detail: Ordinary people had to read a psalm and could only use the escape once. Peers of the realm were exempt from both the literacy test and the one-time limit.
source_title: Academic Kids Encyclopedia: Benefit of clergy

setup: Women in England could only claim 'benefit of clergy' from 1624, and until 1691 only for thefts worth under...
answer: ten shillings, while men got up to forty
detail: Benefit of clergy let some convicts avoid hanging for a first offence. Women only won equal privileges with men in 1691.
source_title: Academic Kids Encyclopedia: Benefit of clergy

setup: A 1571 Act of Parliament required most people in England over the age of six to wear, on Sundays and holidays...
answer: a woollen cap made in England
detail: It was meant to protect the cap-making trade. Nobles, gentlemen and ladies were exempt, offenders were fined three shillings and four pence a day, and it was repealed as unworkable in 1597.

setup: To protect England's wool trade, a law enforced from 1667 until 1814 required every corpse to be...
answer: buried in a shroud of pure sheep's wool
detail: The 'Burying in Woollen' Acts carried a £5 fine, and witnesses had to swear an affidavit that wool alone was used. The law was not formally repealed until 1863.
source_title: Atlas Obscura: England's wool burial shrouds

setup: Under a 1678 Act of Parliament, within eight days of every funeral in England...
answer: two witnesses had to swear the corpse was wrapped only in wool
detail: Written affidavits were required, and clergy recorded the shroud fabric in a register. The law existed to prop up the English wool industry.
source_title: Atlas Obscura: England's wool burial shrouds

setup: Under England's law requiring burial in wool, anyone buried in linen incurred a £5 fine, half of which went to...
detail: The rest went to the poor. Some wealthier families simply paid the fine so their relatives could be buried in linen.
source_title: Institute of Heraldic and Genealogical Studies: Burial in Woollen

setup: England's 1666 law ordering everyone to be buried in a woollen shroud made an exception for...
detail: Ironically, medical guides of the day wrongly claimed wool held the plague infection for years. A stricter version of the law followed in 1678.

setup: In 1795, William Pitt charged a guinea a year for a licence to use hair powder. Those who paid it were mockingly nicknamed...
detail: Reformist Whigs coined the jibe. The Royal Family, their servants and poorly paid clergymen were exempt from the Duty on Hair Powder Act.
source_title: Wikipedia: Duty on Hair Powder Act 1795

setup: Some Whigs protested against the 1795 hair powder tax by cropping their hair short and going unpowdered. The Times mocked them as members of...
detail: Going without powder was also a show of sympathy with revolutionary France. Their short haircut was nicknamed the 'Bedford Level', after the Duke of Bedford.
source_title: Wikipedia: Duty on Hair Powder Act 1795

setup: From 1784 to 1811, every man's hat sold in Britain needed a tax stamp pasted inside the lining. Forging that stamp was punishable by...
detail: Pitt the Younger's hat tax was scaled by the price of the hat, from threepence to two shillings, so it hit the rich hardest.

setup: Under Britain's 1784 hat tax, every hat shop had to buy a licence and display a sign reading...
detail: A licence cost £2 in London and five shillings elsewhere. Each man's hat also needed a revenue stamp inside its lining.

setup: Under medieval English law, a whale washed ashore belonged to the Crown, but it was split so that the king got the head and the queen got...
detail: The jurist Bracton recorded the rule. In Moby-Dick, Melville mocked the old theory that the tail was for the queen's corsets, since whalebone comes from the head.

setup: In 2004, a fisherman who caught a 120 kg sturgeon in Swansea Bay found he legally had to...
answer: tell the Queen, who legally owned it
detail: Sturgeon and whales are 'royal fish' under a 1324 statute of Edward II. Robert Davies was told to use it as he saw fit and gave it to the Natural History Museum.

setup: In Scotland, a stranded whale belongs to the monarch only if it is too big to be hauled ashore by...
answer: a cart pulled by six oxen
detail: In practice that means whales longer than about 25 feet. Marine Scotland collects them on the monarch's behalf.

setup: When the ritual of the Champion riding in and throwing down a gauntlet was dropped from Queen Victoria's coronation, the Champion was compensated with...
detail: Henry Dymoke had performed the challenge at George IV's coronation in 1821, the last time it happened. He was made a baronet in 1841.

setup: The Dymoke family held their Lincolnshire manor of Scrivelsby from the Crown on condition that they...
answer: served as the monarch's champion at coronations
detail: This 'grand serjeanty' tenure meant challenging anyone who disputed the new monarch's right to the throne. The Dymokes have held the role since the 14th century.

setup: In 1698, Peter the Great taxed Russian beards. Men who paid carried a token showing a beard and moustache with the words...
detail: It meant the tax had been paid. Wealthier men got silver tokens and ordinary men copper ones; the tax lasted until 1772, and many tokens were melted down.
source_title: Atlas Obscura: What was the beard tax?

setup: Russian men who kept their beards without paying Peter the Great's beard tax risked...
answer: being forcibly shaved by the police
detail: The tax was formally repealed by Catherine the Great in 1772. It was a financial flop, averaging only about 3,588 roubles a year between 1705 and 1708.

setup: Under Peter the Great's beard tax, rich merchants paid 100 roubles a year, but bearded peasants paid...
answer: a tiny fee every time they entered a city
detail: Rates were set by status: officials paid 60 roubles a year and Muscovites 30. Peasants paid a small sum each time they came into town.

setup: One of the tokens issued to Russians who paid Peter the Great's beard tax bore the blunt motto...
detail: The tokens had a Russian eagle on one side and a beard on the other. They are now rare, probably because people disliked what they stood for.

setup: When Peter the Great forced his courtiers to shave, anyone who was reluctant could expect his New Year's jester to...
detail: Peter returned from Europe determined to modernise Russia, and nobles' beards were shaved at his welcome-home party. The Orthodox Church considered shaving a grave sin.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: Peter the Great's Beard Tax

setup: Peter the Great banned traditional long Russian coats in favour of European jackets. Inspectors were even allowed to...
answer: shorten people's robes right there in the street
detail: Tailors who sold old Russian styles faced steep fines. Peter wanted his subjects to look like Western Europeans.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: Peter the Great's Beard Tax

setup: On his 1697 tour of Europe to study shipbuilding, Tsar Peter the Great travelled incognito, calling himself...
detail: Peter travelled as part of a 'Grand Embassy' and came home determined to Europeanise Russia.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: Peter the Great's Beard Tax

setup: Peter the Great's drinking companions played mock clergymen in a lifelong club called...
detail: Its full name added 'of Fools and Jesters'. It had a mock 'Prince-Pope', and Peter himself took the humble rank of 'Deacon'.
source_title: JSTOR Daily: Peter the Great's Beard Tax

setup: Peter the Great's 1704 rouble, worth exactly 100 kopeks, made Russia...
answer: the first country with a decimal currency
detail: The rouble was set equal to a silver thaler.
source_title: American Numismatic Society: The Reign of Peter the Great

setup: Every year the City of London pays the Crown rent on a long-vanished forge near the Strand. The payment is...
detail: The official counts them and declares 'Good number'. The same horseshoes and nails are then lent back to the City for next year.
source_title: Historic UK: The Ceremony of Quit Rents

setup: Since 1211, the City of London has paid the Crown rent for a patch of Shropshire land with...
answer: a blunt billhook and a sharp axe
detail: The King's Remembrancer tests them on a hazel stick: the billhook should barely mark it, the axe splits it. He then declares 'Good service'.
source_title: Historic UK: The Ceremony of Quit Rents

setup: When the City of London pays its rent to the Crown for Southwark, a jury foreman stacks the coins on a chequered cloth and declares...
detail: The rent is £11, paid in old five-shilling crowns. The chequered cloth is said to be where the word 'Exchequer' comes from.

setup: For over 700 years, coins from the Royal Mint have been put on trial to check they are up to scratch, judged by...
detail: The ceremony is called the Trial of the Pyx. The jury is sworn in by the King's Remembrancer and the trial now takes place at Goldsmiths' Hall.

setup: The post of King's Remembrancer, created by Henry II in 1154 to keep track of unpaid taxes, is considered...
answer: England's oldest judicial office still in existence
detail: The first holder was Richard of Ilchester. Today the Remembrancer presides over quaint ceremonies like the City of London's quit rents.

setup: Under a 1291 deed, London's Brewers' Company paid rent for the land under its hall every Midsummer's Day with...
detail: They hung it on the hall gate for the heirs of a goldsmith, at a cost of eightpence. They kept paying even after the heirs vanished, until about 1550.
source_title: Brewers' Hall: A Rose Garland at Midsummer

setup: In 897, Pope Stephen VI put his predecessor, Pope Formosus, on trial for perjury, even though Formosus...
answer: had been dead for nine months
detail: At the 'Cadaver Synod', the corpse was dug up and propped on a throne while a deacon answered on its behalf. It was found guilty.

setup: After the corpse of Pope Formosus was found guilty in 897, it was stripped of its robes, lost three fingers, and eventually...
answer: was thrown into the River Tiber
detail: The body washed up and rumours of miracles spread. A later pope annulled the trial and had Formosus reburied in St Peter's.

setup: In 2002, a man from Bury St Edmunds, fined £25 by the DVLA over his motorbike, asked to settle the matter by...
answer: trial by combat against a DVLA champion
detail: Leon Humphries argued that the ancient right still existed. Magistrates refused and fined him £200.

setup: In 1396, a Highland clan feud was settled in Perth by a staged fight between teams of about thirty men. Of the sixty who fought...
detail: The 'Battle of the Clans' was fought on the North Inch in front of King Robert III. Historians still argue over which clans actually took part.

setup: In 2020, an American man fighting a custody case formally asked the court for...
detail: David Zachary Ostrom later admitted the request was a stunt to attract media attention. It wasn't granted.

setup: To avoid Britain's 1712 tax on patterned wallpaper, many householders...
answer: bought plain paper and stencilled the patterns themselves
detail: The tax started at a penny a square yard and rose to a shilling by 1809. It was abolished in 1836.

setup: When Britain taxed bricks by the thousand from 1784, manufacturers fought back by...
detail: In 1801 the government capped brick moulds at 10 x 5 x 3 inches and doubled the tax on larger ones. The brick tax was abolished in 1850.

setup: In 1807, taxpayers in Ohio had to hand in, along with their taxes...
detail: The quota was set in proportion to each person's county tax, from 10 to 100 scalps, and handed to the township clerk with the payment.
source_title: Family Tree Magazine: 10 Weird Taxes Our Ancestors Paid

setup: Alabama taxed every pack of playing cards from 1935 until 2015, when it was scrapped because...
answer: collecting it cost more than it raised
detail: Each pack needed a ten-cent revenue stamp. A new law suspended taxes whose collection costs exceeded their revenue.
source_title: Family Tree Magazine: 10 Weird Taxes Our Ancestors Paid

setup: The ace of spades is traditionally the fanciest card in a British pack because...
answer: it carried proof that the card tax was paid
detail: From 1712 the duty stamp went on the ace of spades, and from 1765 the Stamp Office printed an official ace. The tax on cards lasted until 1960.

setup: In 1805, a licensed card-maker named Richard Harding was sentenced to hang at the Old Bailey for forging...
answer: the tax stamp on the ace of spades
detail: He also faked the duty labels on card wrappers and knowingly sold the fakes. Pleas for a reprieve failed, and he was executed in November 1805.

setup: The 1736 Gin Act demanded a £50 licence to sell gin. Six years later, the number of licences bought was...
detail: Meanwhile gin production rose by almost 50% thanks to bootlegging. The licence cost more than a labourer earned in a year.
source_title: Institute of Economic Affairs: Stupid taxes are nothing new

setup: The holy oil for Elizabeth II's anointing in 1953 had to be remade from scratch because the old batch was...
answer: destroyed in a wartime bombing raid
detail: The firm that made it had closed, but an elderly relative had kept a few ounces of the original base, from which a new batch was made.

setup: Thomas Hicks, the official winner of the 1904 Olympic marathon, was kept going in the final miles by his support team feeding him egg whites, brandy and...
answer: strychnine, a poison then used as a stimulant
detail: It was legal at the time. Hicks won in 3 hours 28 minutes, still the slowest winning time in Olympic marathon history, was practically carried over the line and never ran a marathon again.
source_title: Olympics.com: The strange case of the St Louis 1904 marathon

setup: Cuban runner Félix Carvajal still managed to finish fourth in the 1904 Olympic marathon, despite stopping during the race to...
answer: eat some rotten apples and have a nap
detail: Carvajal ran in street clothes cut down into shorts and had reportedly gone about 40 hours without eating. The apples gave him cramps, so he lay down for a sleep.

setup: The organiser of the 1904 Olympic marathon allowed just one water source along the route in 32°C heat, claiming he was researching...
detail: Only 14 of the 32 starters finished. One runner was found unconscious, his insides damaged by dust kicked up by officials' cars.

setup: In March 1958, a family in Mars Bluff, South Carolina, lost their vegetable garden and their daughters' playhouse when...
answer: a US Air Force bomber accidentally dropped an atomic bomb there
detail: A crewman grabbed the emergency release while looking for a faulty pin. The nuclear core was stored elsewhere, so only the conventional explosive went off. The family later received $54,000.

setup: Unable to get affordable life insurance, the Apollo 11 astronauts provided for their families by...
answer: signing hundreds of envelopes for them to sell if they died
detail: Known as 'insurance covers', they were postmarked on launch day or landing day to boost their value. Crews up to Apollo 16 did the same.

setup: After coming back from the Moon in 1969, Armstrong, Aldrin and Collins signed a customs form at Honolulu Airport that gave their flight route as...
answer: Cape Kennedy to Honolulu, with a stopover on the Moon
detail: Their cargo was declared as moon rock and moon dust samples. NASA confirmed the form was genuine but called it 'a little joke at the time'.
source_title: Space.com: Apollo astronauts had to go through customs

setup: Australian Prime Minister Harold Holt vanished while swimming off a Victoria beach in 1967. Among the things later named in his memory was...
answer: a public swimming centre in Melbourne
detail: The Harold Holt Memorial Swimming Centre in Glen Iris was being built when he disappeared and was named after him as the local MP. His body was never found.

setup: Because Prime Minister Harold Holt disappeared off a beach in 1967, Australians use the phrase 'doing a Harold Holt' to mean...
detail: It is rhyming slang: Holt rhymes with bolt. Holt was swimming in rough seas at Cheviot Beach and was presumed drowned.

setup: When a 1983 book claimed Australian PM Harold Holt had faked his death to defect to China by submarine, his widow Zara dismissed it by saying...
answer: he didn't even like Chinese food
detail: Journalist Anthony Grey's book was widely criticised for errors. A 2005 inquest found Holt simply took an unnecessary risk and drowned in rough water.

setup: In 1969 the US Navy launched the USS Harold E. Holt, named after the drowned Australian PM. It was the first American warship ever named after...
detail: It was a destroyer escort. Holt is also remembered by a plaque bolted to the seabed off the beach where he vanished.

setup: A Second World War plan to firebomb Japan using bats fitted with tiny incendiary bombs ended up...
answer: setting fire to an American air base
detail: In May 1943 armed bats escaped at Carlsbad's auxiliary air base in New Mexico and roosted under a fuel tank. The idea came from a dentist, Lytle Adams.

setup: During the Second World War, psychologist B.F. Skinner designed a guided missile that would be steered by...
answer: three pigeons pecking at screens in its nose cone
detail: The pigeons were trained to peck at an image of the target, which nudged the missile's course. The nose cone is now in the Smithsonian's American History Museum.

setup: In 1943, Britain and Canada seriously explored building a gigantic aircraft carrier made out of...
detail: The material, 'pykrete', was invented by Geoffrey Pyke and was far tougher than plain ice. The scheme was called Project Habakkuk.

setup: In 1943 a secret prototype for an ice aircraft carrier was built on Patricia Lake in Canada. The work was done by...
answer: conscientious objectors who had no idea what it was
detail: The project was dropped as too costly, and the model was left to melt over about three summers. Its remains still lie at the bottom of the lake.

setup: In the Second World War, Britain's Special Operations Executive filled dead rats with plastic explosive, hoping German workers would...
detail: The first batch was intercepted, so they were never used. But the Germans wasted so much effort hunting for more that the SOE counted it a success.

setup: In 1944, Scottish spiritualist medium Helen Duncan was sentenced to nine months at the Old Bailey under...
detail: She is usually described as the last person in Britain jailed under the witchcraft law. Churchill called the case 'obsolete tomfoolery', and the Act was repealed in 1951.

setup: In 1944, Polish soldiers told that pets weren't allowed on their troop ship from Egypt to Italy got round the rule by...
detail: Wojtek the bear was given a rank, a service number and a pay book. He reportedly carried ammunition crates at Monte Cassino and was later made a corporal.

setup: Wojtek, the bear who served with the Polish army in the Second World War, was bought as a cub from a shepherd boy in Iran in exchange for...
answer: tins of food, chocolate and a Swiss army knife
detail: Soldiers found the orphaned cub in 1942. He grew to around six feet tall, loved beer and wrestling, and retired to Edinburgh Zoo.

setup: Simon, the ship's cat on HMS Amethyst in 1949, was promoted to 'Able Seacat' after killing a rat the crew had nicknamed...
detail: Despite being wounded in the Yangtze Incident, Simon kept hunting rats. He remains the only cat awarded the Dickin Medal, the animal Victoria Cross.

setup: In October 1963, France launched a rocket from the Sahara Desert carrying the world's first...
detail: Félicette, a black-and-white cat, survived a 13-minute flight. She was picked from 14 female cats given numbers instead of names. A statue of her was unveiled in 2019.

setup: In 1965 astronaut John Young caused a stir in Congress after smuggling aboard the Gemini 3 spacecraft...
detail: Wally Schirra had it made at a Cocoa Beach restaurant. Crumbs floated round the cabin, and a senior NASA official promised Congress to prevent 'recurrence of corned beef sandwiches'.
source_title: Smithsonian National Air and Space Museum

setup: Gus Grissom nicknamed his 1965 Gemini spacecraft 'Molly Brown', after the musical The Unsinkable Molly Brown, because his previous capsule had...
detail: His Mercury capsule Liberty Bell 7 sank in 1961. Gemini 3 was its official name, but 'Molly Brown' stuck as the nickname.

setup: On Apollo 14 in 1971, astronaut Stuart Roosa, a former forest firefighter, took to lunar orbit and back a canister holding thousands of...
answer: tree seeds, later grown into 'Moon Trees'
detail: About 500 seeds each of five species flew. Their bags burst in a vacuum chamber during decontamination, so the seeds had to be gathered and sorted by hand.
source_title: NASA: Stuart Roosa and the Moon Tree Seeds

setup: The Apollo 15 crew landed in hot water with Congress after it emerged they had secretly taken to the Moon...
answer: hundreds of unauthorised envelopes for a stamp dealer
detail: They carried about 400 unofficial postal covers to the lunar surface, 100 of which went to West German dealer Hermann Sieger. The crew faced a closed Senate committee session and never flew in space again.
source_title: Today I Found Out: Apollo astronaut insurance

setup: On Christmas Day 1950, four Glasgow students took the Stone of Scone from Westminster Abbey, and in the process...
answer: dropped it and broke it in two
detail: A Glasgow councillor and stonemason mended it. In April 1951 it turned up on the site of the High Altar at Arbroath Abbey.
source_title: Wikipedia: 1950 removal of the Stone of Scone

setup: In 1914, the Coronation Chair in Westminster Abbey was damaged by...
detail: Members of the Women's Social and Political Union planted it. The blast probably cracked the Stone of Scone too, though that wasn't noticed for decades.
source_title: Mental Floss: Stone of Scone facts

setup: In March 1966, months before England hosted the World Cup, the Jules Rimet trophy was stolen from Westminster Central Hall, where it was on show at...
detail: It was on display at Stampex, run by Stanley Gibbons, despite guards being present. A dog called Pickles found it a week later.
source_title: Wikipedia: 1966 theft of the Jules Rimet Trophy

setup: When police met a man demanding a ransom for the stolen World Cup trophy in 1966, the payment they brought was...
answer: bundles of plain paper with real notes only on top
detail: Edward Betchley, posing as 'Jackson' at the handover in Battersea Park, didn't spot the trick but grew suspicious. He jumped from the moving police car and was chased down and arrested.
source_title: Wikipedia: 1966 theft of the Jules Rimet Trophy

setup: As a reward for finding the stolen World Cup trophy in 1966, Pickles the dog received a medal and...
answer: an invitation to England's victory banquet
detail: Pickles sniffed out the trophy wrapped in newspaper in Upper Norwood, south London. His owner received nearly £5,000 in rewards.

setup: In the 1962 film Dr. No, James Bond pauses in the villain's lair to look at...
answer: a Goya painting stolen in real life the year before
detail: Goya's portrait of the Duke of Wellington had been taken from the National Gallery in 1961, so the film joked that Dr No had it.

setup: In 1965, four years after it was stolen from the National Gallery, Goya's portrait of Wellington was recovered from...
answer: a left-luggage office at Birmingham New Street station
detail: Kempton Bunton sent the Daily Mirror the left-luggage ticket after the paper printed a message he had asked for. It alerted police instead of meeting his demands.

setup: The world's first cash machine opened at Barclays in Enfield in June 1967, and the first person to withdraw money from it was...
detail: He took out the maximum of £10. There were no plastic cards: customers fed in special paper cheques laced with mildly radioactive carbon-14.

setup: John Shepherd-Barron, inventor of the cash machine, originally wanted six-digit PINs, but settled on four because...
answer: his wife said four was all she could remember
detail: His machine opened at Barclays in Enfield in 1967. The branch marked the 50th anniversary by turning one of its cash machines gold.

setup: The world's first webcam, set up at Cambridge University's Computer Laboratory in 1991, was pointed at...
detail: Researchers on other floors wanted to know if there was fresh coffee before making the trip. The images went on the web in 1993.

setup: When Cambridge's famous webcam coffee pot was switched off in 2001, it was sold on eBay for £3,350 to...
detail: Krups staff refurbished the machine free of charge and it was switched on again in the magazine's editorial office. Since 2016 it has been on loan to a computer museum in Paderborn.

setup: In January 1919, 21 people in Boston were killed and around 150 injured by...
answer: a wave of molasses from a burst tank
detail: Millions of gallons surged through the streets at about 35 mph. Locals said the area smelled of molasses for years.

setup: In 1962, at least 14 schools in what is now Tanzania were forced to close because of an epidemic of...
detail: It began at a girls' boarding school in Kashasha and affected about 1,000 people. It is regarded as a case of mass hysteria.

setup: In 1949, Big Ben's clock was slowed down by four and a half minutes when...
answer: a flock of starlings perched on the minute hand
detail: Their combined weight was enough to hold back the hand. Big Ben's timekeeping has also been upset by snow, ice and wartime bomb damage.
source_title: Mental Floss: 15 things about Big Ben

setup: On New Year's Eve 1962, the rest of Britain saw in the new year before Big Ben because its first bong came...
answer: about ten minutes late, thanks to snow on the hands
detail: Heavy snow and ice weighed down the clock's hands, delaying the chimes rather than stopping them.

setup: In April 1945, the German submarine U-1206 had to surface and be scuttled off Scotland after a crew member...
detail: Sewage and seawater flooded the batteries, creating chlorine gas. With British aircraft overhead the sub couldn't dive again; four men died.

setup: In 1956, Grumman test pilot Tom Attridge fired his jet's cannon during a steep dive and ended up...
answer: shooting himself down with his own bullets
detail: The cannon rounds slowed down while his diving jet kept speed and caught them, hitting its windscreen, nose and engine intake. He crash-landed in trees short of the runway and survived.

setup: In July 1945 the Brazilian cruiser Bahia sank in three minutes after a gunner, shooting at a target kite during practice...
answer: followed it down and hit the ship's own depth charges
detail: Accounts differ, but only around 30 of more than 370 aboard were rescued. Torpedo rumours persist, but US and Brazilian naval inquiries blamed the gunnery accident.

setup: In 1958, after a mid-air collision, a US bomber dumped a 7,600-pound nuclear bomb into the sea near Tybee Island, Georgia, where...
detail: Searches in 1958 and 2004 came up empty. The Air Force says its nuclear capsule had been removed, though later testimony has questioned this.

setup: Russia's 1915 Tsar Tank looked like a giant tricycle with front wheels almost 30 feet across. In its first test, it...
answer: got stuck in soft ground and was abandoned
detail: It sat where it stuck for years and was finally scrapped in 1923.

setup: Britain's wartime Panjandrum was a drum of explosives between two ten-foot wooden wheels, designed to be driven up beaches by...
detail: The rockets kept detaching and sending it off course. In its final test it nearly ploughed into spectators, and the project was cancelled.

setup: In 1944, Germany developed the Krummlauf, a curved barrel attachment for rifles that let soldiers...
detail: It used a periscope sight. The bent barrels wore out after a few hundred rounds and bullets often broke up.

setup: Big Babylon, the 'supergun' Saddam Hussein commissioned in the late 1980s, was designed with a barrel...
detail: Engineered by Gerald Bull, it was officially meant to fire payloads into orbit. Being immobile, it would have given its position away the moment it fired.

setup: In 1944 and 1945, Japan attacked mainland North America with thousands of...
detail: The hydrogen balloons rode the jet stream across the Pacific. Remnants were found in around 17 US states, Canada and Mexico.

setup: In the 1950s, US Army scientists at Edgewood Arsenal developed a chemical weapon designed to...
detail: The agent, BZ, causes delirium and hallucinations, and was later loaded into cluster bombs. It was dropped from the arsenal because its effects on troops were too unpredictable.

setup: American Margaret Abbott won a women's golf tournament in Paris in 1900, apparently without realising...
answer: it was part of the Olympic Games
detail: That made her the first American woman to win an Olympic event, an honour she reportedly never knew about.

setup: Between 1912 and 1948, as well as for sport, the Olympics awarded medals for...
detail: The idea came from Pierre de Coubertin, and categories included architecture, literature and sculpture. The contests were dropped because most of the artists were professionals.
