setup: When Nadia Comăneci scored gymnastics' first perfect 10 at the 1976 Olympics, the scoreboard showed...
detail: The board only went up to 9.99, as nobody expected a perfect score. She went on to score seven perfect 10s at those Games.

setup: Around 1960, Richard James, the inventor of the Slinky, walked out on his wife, six children and his toy company to...
answer: join a Bible-translation mission in Bolivia
detail: He went to work with the evangelical Wycliffe Bible Translators. His wife Betty took over, mortgaged her house to promote the toy, and ran the company until 1998.

setup: The Slinky was born in 1943, when shipyard engineer Richard James was trying to design a spring that would...
answer: stop delicate ship instruments being jostled at sea
detail: Working at Cramp Shipbuilding in Philadelphia, he saw a dropped coil 'shimmy' across the floor. His wife Betty picked the name from a dictionary.

setup: In 1957, two engineers sealed air bubbles between two sheets of plastic. Before it became packaging, they tried selling it as...
detail: Al Fielding and Marc Chavannes also tried marketing it as greenhouse insulation. Neither idea took off until it was pitched as protective packaging.
source_title: Mental Floss: Bubble Wrap was supposed to be wallpaper

setup: Bubble wrap flopped as wallpaper and as greenhouse insulation. Its first big customer, who finally made it a success, was...
answer: IBM, to protect a new computer in transit
detail: A Sealed Air salesman, Frederick Bowers, pitched it as packaging, and IBM used it to ship its 1401 computer.
source_title: Mental Floss: Bubble Wrap was supposed to be wallpaper

setup: Fred Baur, the chemist who invented the Pringles tube, also helped to develop...
detail: Baur worked for Procter & Gamble on frying oils and other food technology. He filed his patent for the stacked-crisp tube in 1966.

setup: When a gardener at Newstead Abbey, Lord Byron's family home, dug up a well-preserved human skull, the poet had it made into...
detail: Newstead was a former priory. Byron even wrote a poem about it: 'Lines Inscribed Upon a Cup Formed from a Skull'.

setup: 'The Vampyre', the 1819 story often credited with launching the vampire genre, was written by Lord Byron's doctor, John Polidori, but it was first published...
detail: It grew from a fragment Byron wrote during the 1816 Lake Geneva ghost-story contest that also produced Frankenstein. Its vampire, Lord Ruthven, is often read as a portrait of Byron.

setup: After Lord Byron died in 1824, his friends and his publisher decided his memoirs should be...
answer: burned, because they were 'fit only for a brothel'
detail: It happened in publisher John Murray's fireplace. Murray's reader William Gifford reportedly called them 'fit only for a brothel'; Thomas Moore objected but was overruled, and no copy survives.

setup: Byron's daughter Ada Lovelace, credited with writing the first computer algorithm, died of cancer at the age of 36, which was...
answer: the same age her father was when he died
detail: Byron died in 1824 aged 36, when Ada was only eight. She was his only legitimate child.

setup: When Kempton Bunton was tried for taking Goya's portrait of the Duke of Wellington from the National Gallery, he was cleared of stealing the painting but convicted of stealing...
detail: His defence argued he never meant to keep the painting, so it wasn't theft. The frame was never recovered, and he got three months in prison.
source_title: The National Archives: The story behind The Duke

setup: After Goya's Duke of Wellington vanished from the National Gallery in 1961, the thief's ransom note demanded £140,000, which was...
answer: exactly what the government had paid for it
detail: Kempton Bunton wrote the notes; his son John later confessed to taking it. Bunton cut his demand to £5,000 in 1963, then suggested a charity exhibition.
source_title: The National Archives: The story behind The Duke

setup: Months after Scottish students took the Stone of Destiny from Westminster Abbey in 1950, it finally turned up...
answer: left at the ruins of Arbroath Abbey
detail: It was taken back to Westminster on 11 April 1951. None of the students was ever charged.
source_title: University of Glasgow: The daring capture of the Stone of Destiny

setup: When police questioned Kay Matheson, getaway driver in the 1950 Stone of Destiny raid, she told them the stone was...
detail: It wasn't. She broke two toes during the raid, and no charges were brought against her or the other students.

setup: From 1934 to 1947, Webster's dictionary listed 'dord' as a word meaning density. It got in because...
answer: someone misread a note saying 'D or d'
detail: The slip meant density could be abbreviated D or d. An editor spotted the 'ghost word' in 1939, but it wasn't removed until the 1947 printing.

setup: The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia featured Robert Dayton, a blind American artist famous for...
answer: 'Aroma-Art', exposing audiences to scented air in a sealed chamber
detail: Dayton was a fake entry, planted alongside the equally fictional photographer Lillian Mountweazel to catch anyone copying the encyclopedia.

setup: In the 1930s, mapmakers invented a fake New York hamlet called Agloe to catch copiers. The trap backfired when...
answer: someone built a real shop there and named it after the map
detail: Agloe came from the mapmakers' initials, Ernest Alpens and Otto Lindberg. The Agloe General Store made the fictional place real enough to feature in John Green's Paper Towns.

setup: Germany's leading medical dictionary, the Pschyrembel, includes an entry for the 'stone louse', a tiny creature that supposedly...
detail: Invented by the comedian Loriot, it was removed in 1996 but restored in 1997, with a new section on its role in the fall of the Berlin Wall.

setup: A 1943 Webster's dictionary described the jungftak, a Persian bird in which the male and female each had only one wing, and could fly only by...
detail: One bird supposedly had a bone hook and the other a bone eyelet. The jungftak is entirely fictional.

setup: A respected German classics encyclopedia included 'apopudobalia', an ancient Roman sport that was...
answer: basically football, and completely made up
detail: It appeared in Der neue Pauly in 1996. One reviewer missed the joke and published a rebuttal listing six supposed mistakes in the entry.

setup: In the early 1970s, some American county maps showed Mount Richard, a peak on the continental divide that was...
answer: thought to have been slipped in by a draughtsman called Richard
detail: Draughtsman Richard Ciacci is believed to have added it, and the mountain's non-existence went unnoticed for two years.

setup: Michigan's official 1978 state map showed two Ohio towns, Beatosu and Goblu, which were...
answer: fake, invented as a college sports rivalry joke
detail: Read aloud, the names say 'Beat OSU' and 'Go Blue', a dig at Ohio State from Michigan fans.

setup: At the 1974 NHL draft, the Buffalo Sabres ice hockey team picked a Japanese forward named Taro Tsujimoto. The catch was...
detail: Sabres general manager Punch Imlach invented the player to fool the league.

setup: George P. Burdell appears in Georgia Tech's records as a football letterman in the late 1920s and a basketball player in the 1950s, despite...
answer: being a student prank who never existed
detail: He was invented as a prank in 1927 and listed in the 1928 to 1930 football and 1955 to 1958 basketball guides.

setup: In 2019, the lyrics site Genius said it caught Google reprinting its song lyrics thanks to apostrophes that secretly spelled out...
detail: Genius used a pattern of different apostrophe styles in its transcriptions; read as dots and dashes, they formed a hidden message.

setup: In the 1970s, the US Army asked soldiers to rate foods including funistrada, buttered ermal and braised trake, which were...
answer: fake dishes to catch people not paying attention
detail: The made-up items were controls: anyone rating them was clearly filling in the survey without thinking.

setup: Samuel Johnson's famous dictionary included the non-word 'foupe', because he...
answer: mistook an old-fashioned long 's' for an 'f'
detail: The word he was copying was 'soupe'. The Victorian scholar W.W. Skeat later coined the term 'ghost word' for such phantoms.

setup: Several dictionaries once listed the word 'kime', which only existed because a typo in the Edinburgh Review had mangled the word...
detail: Lexicographers copied the misprint in good faith, giving the phantom word a life of its own.

setup: In 1726, an English servant named Mary Toft convinced a surgeon to the royal household that she had given birth to...
detail: Nathaniel St André, surgeon to George I's household, published a pamphlet backing her. She confessed on 7 December 1726.

setup: Mary Toft's 1726 claim to be giving birth to rabbits unravelled when an investigator discovered her husband had been...
detail: A porter also confessed that Toft's sister-in-law had bribed him to smuggle a rabbit into her room.

setup: In 1835, the New York Sun reported that an astronomer had seen life on the Moon, including bison, two-legged beavers and...
detail: The real astronomer named, Sir John Herschel, knew nothing about it. Writer Richard Adams Locke later admitted inventing the series as satire.
source_title: Museum of Hoaxes: The Great Moon Hoax

setup: The 1835 'Great Moon Hoax' told readers that the Moon was home to beavers that walked on two legs and...
detail: The story ran in six instalments in the New York Sun, falsely credited to the astronomer Sir John Herschel.
source_title: Museum of Hoaxes: The Great Moon Hoax

setup: In 1925, conman Victor Lustig sold the Eiffel Tower for scrap by posing as an official from...
answer: the French Ministry of Posts and Telegraphs
detail: He'd read about the tower's rising upkeep costs. Businessman André Poisson paid a bribe and about 70,000 francs before Lustig fled to Austria.

setup: Conman Victor Lustig once took $50,000 from Al Capone for a crooked investment, then...
answer: gave it all back two months later
detail: He kept the money in a safe deposit box, returned it saying the deal had failed, then talked Capone into a handout of $5,000 (some say $1,000).

setup: Victor Lustig sold a mahogany 'money box' that supposedly copied any banknote, with one catch: each copy took...
detail: He secretly loaded the box with genuine notes so the demonstration worked, then sold it for a fortune.

setup: When Colonel Thomas Blood tried to steal the Crown Jewels in 1671, he made the crown easier to carry off by...
detail: Blood was disguised as a parson. An accomplice hid the orb by stuffing it down his breeches.
source_title: History.com: The man who stole the Crown Jewels

setup: After being caught stealing the Crown Jewels in 1671, Thomas Blood wasn't executed. Instead, Charles II...
answer: pardoned him and gave him land in Ireland
detail: The land was worth £500 a year. Historians still debate why; theories include the King liking a daring rogue or using Blood as a spy.
source_title: History.com: The man who stole the Crown Jewels

setup: Questioned by Charles II himself, Crown Jewels thief Thomas Blood admitted he had once planned to kill the King while he was...
detail: Blood claimed he had changed his mind. He refused to talk to anyone but the King, and was pardoned anyway.
source_title: History Hit: Thomas Blood and the Crown Jewels

setup: When Vincenzo Peruggia stole the Mona Lisa in 1911 and found his exit door locked, he was let out by...
detail: Peruggia wore a white staff smock. He had unscrewed the doorknob, and a plumber named Sauvet obligingly opened the door with pliers.
source_title: History Hit: The theft of the Mona Lisa

setup: After the Mona Lisa vanished from the Louvre in 1911, nobody raised the alarm for over a day, because staff assumed...
detail: Artist Louis Béroud finally asked where it was, about 26 hours later. The Louvre closed and France shut its borders.
source_title: History Hit: The theft of the Mona Lisa

setup: Among the people questioned by police over the 1911 theft of the Mona Lisa was...
detail: His friend, the poet Guillaume Apollinaire, was arrested first. Neither was involved: the thief was Vincenzo Peruggia, who had worked at the Louvre.
source_title: History Hit: The theft of the Mona Lisa

setup: Mona Lisa thief Vincenzo Peruggia claimed he was taking the painting home to Italy, wrongly believing it had been stolen by...
detail: In fact it had reached France more than two centuries before Napoleon was born. Peruggia served only seven months.
source_title: History Hit: The theft of the Mona Lisa

setup: To make sure his 1939 novel Gadsby contained no letter E in over 50,000 words, author Ernest Vincent Wright said he...
answer: tied down the E key on his typewriter
detail: Even so, four Es slipped into the first printing, including 'the' three times.

setup: In June 1958, Cambridge students hoisted an Austin Seven car onto the roof of the Senate House. Unable to get it down, the authorities eventually...
answer: cut it into pieces with blowtorches
detail: Thirteen Gonville and Caius students planned the stunt for over a year. Officials tried for five days before cutting the car into six pieces.
source_title: Oxford Royale: Amazing anecdotes of Cambridge life

setup: In the 1960s, Cambridge students bought a wrecked Austin Seven for £2, floated it down the River Cam on four punts, and...
answer: hung it from the Bridge of Sighs
detail: It came five years after the Senate House car stunt. The garage owner had already sold the engine for £5, and the 1831 bridge was undamaged.
source_title: Oxford Royale: Amazing anecdotes of Cambridge life

setup: In 1905, the Mayor of Cambridge gave a grand tour to a party of visitors supposedly from the Sultan of Zanzibar, who were actually...
detail: The hoax was by Horace de Vere Cole and Adrian Stephen. Five years later Cole tricked the Royal Navy aboard HMS Dreadnought, with Virginia Woolf disguised as Abyssinian royalty.
source_title: Oxford Royale: Amazing anecdotes of Cambridge life

setup: Before it became a children's modelling toy, Play-Doh was sold as...
detail: The flour-based putty was made by Kutol Products for cleaning soot off wallpaper, and was relaunched as a children's toy in the 1950s.

setup: While testing microwave cooking, engineer Percy Spencer put an egg in a kettle under a magnetron, and it...
detail: Spencer also made the first microwave popcorn. Legend has it he got the idea when a sweet in his pocket melted near a radar set.

setup: The first commercial microwave oven, launched in 1947, stood about six feet tall and cost around...
detail: Affordable countertop models didn't arrive until 1967, when Amana launched the Radarange.

setup: A hollowed-out stone lamp-post in Trafalgar Square once served as a tiny police box for watching demonstrations. If the officer inside picked up its phone...
answer: the lamp on top started flashing to summon help
detail: The box was built in the 1920s so police could keep watch over protests. Legend claims the lamp came from HMS Victory, but that is not true.
source_title: Historic UK: Britain's Smallest Police Station

setup: Savoy Court, the short approach to London's Savoy Hotel off the Strand, breaks a basic rule of British roads: cars there must...
detail: Vehicles enter via the right-hand lane, contrary to normal UK rules. Most accounts trace the arrangement to an Act of Parliament in 1902.
source_title: Londonist: Is the Savoy really the only place?

setup: The elegant houses at 23 and 24 Leinster Gardens in Bayswater have porches, balconies and windows, but if you knocked on the door you would find...
answer: they're a fake front hiding an open-air railway line
detail: The houses were demolished for the Underground in the 1860s, and steam trains needed open track to vent smoke. The five-foot-thick facade has painted-on windows and doors with no letterboxes.
source_title: Atlas Obscura: Leinster Gardens False Facades

setup: A Victorian time capsule sealed beneath Cleopatra's Needle on London's Embankment contains Bibles, a railway guide, a razor, children's toys and...
detail: The cache also holds a portrait of Queen Victoria, coins, ladies' clothing and that day's Times. Six sailors died during the obelisk's stormy voyage from Egypt.

setup: In 2012 the Perthshire village of Dull formally paired up with a town in Oregon called...
detail: Bland Shire in New South Wales joined them in 2013, forming what was billed as the 'League of Extraordinary Communities'. Dull has well under a hundred residents.

setup: Boring in Oregon is not named for being dull. It actually takes its name from...
answer: William Harrison Boring, a Union Civil War veteran who settled there
detail: Boring fought at the Siege of Vicksburg before settling in the area. The town's post office took the name in 1903, and its motto is 'The most exciting place to live!'

setup: Westward Ho! has one exclamation mark, but a town in Quebec beats it with two. It is called...
detail: The Quebec town has two exclamation marks in its name. Countryfile notes it is the only town in the world with two.

setup: To make the Great Clock in the Elizabeth Tower, home of Big Ben, run faster or slower, its keepers...
answer: stack old pennies on the pendulum
detail: Adding or removing coins shifts the pendulum's centre of mass. Pre-decimal pennies have been used since 1859, and a £5 Crown coin was later added.
source_title: CoinNews: £5 Crown keeps Big Ben on time

setup: On 23 October 1843, fourteen men climbed to the top of the newly built Nelson's Column and...
answer: ate a rump steak dinner with champagne
detail: The steaks were hauled up by pulley and reportedly arrived still hot. Retellings often call the diners stonemasons, though newspapers at the time did not say so.
source_title: Londonist: Dinner for 14 on Nelson's Column

setup: On 1 April 1977, bookseller Richard Booth marked the 'independence' of the Welsh border town of Hay-on-Wye by declaring himself...
detail: The town had proclaimed its independence that January as a publicity stunt. It helped make Hay famous as a 'town of books'.

setup: In 1915 a barrister called Cecil Chubb went to an auction in Salisbury and came home having bought...
detail: He paid £6,600 for lot 15. Legend says his wife had sent him to buy dining chairs; in 1918 he gave the monument to the nation and was later made a baronet.
source_title: Smithsonian: A Man Once Bought Stonehenge for his Wife

setup: When Cecil Chubb gave Stonehenge to the nation in 1918, one of his conditions was that...
answer: local people should always be let in free
detail: He also capped the admission fee at one shilling. Locals still visit for free today.
source_title: Smithsonian: A Man Once Bought Stonehenge for his Wife

setup: The 58-letter name of the Anglesey village Llanfairpwllgwyngyllgogerychwyrndrobwllllantysiliogogogoch is thought to have been invented in the 1860s...
answer: as a publicity stunt for the railway station
detail: The idea was to give it the longest station name in Britain. Sir John Morris-Jones said a local tailor dreamed it up.

setup: The final 'gogogoch' in the famous long Welsh village name means 'red cave'. Oddly, it was probably borrowed from...
answer: a parish in Cardiganshire, not anything nearby
detail: Most of the name describes real local features, like St Mary's church and a fierce whirlpool in the Menai Strait. The red cave ending is thought to have been inspired by a parish elsewhere in Wales.

setup: After their village sign was stolen once too often, residents of Shitterton in Dorset clubbed together in 2010 and replaced it with...
answer: a 1.5-tonne block of carved Purbeck stone
detail: Households chipped in £20 each and volunteers used a crane to place it. The name comes from Old English for a stream used as an open sewer.

setup: The Victorians tried to rename the Dorset hamlet of Shitterton because its name meant 'farmstead on the stream used as an open sewer'. Their suggested new name was...
detail: The polite version never stuck. The name dates back at least to the Domesday Book of 1086, where it appears as Scatera.

setup: Temple Bar, the old Wren gateway into the City of London, was taken down stone by stone in the 1870s and spent over a century...
answer: on a country estate in Hertfordshire
detail: It was rebuilt at Theobalds Park, where Lady Meux entertained Edward VII and Winston Churchill in the room above the arch. It returned to the City at Paternoster Square in 2004.

setup: Throughout the 18th century, the iron spikes on top of London's Temple Bar gateway were used to display...
detail: The gateway stood where Fleet Street meets the Strand. It now stands beside St Paul's Cathedral in Paternoster Square.

setup: On the Dunmore estate near Falkirk stands a 14-metre stone garden building, built for the Earl of Dunmore in the shape of...
detail: Pineapples were a costly status symbol, and the walled garden's hothouses were used to grow them. Today you can rent it as a holiday home through the Landmark Trust.

setup: In 1929 the owner of Lundy Island in the Bristol Channel issued his own coins, called Puffins, and as a result he was...
detail: Martin Coles Harman was convicted under the Coinage Act 1870 and lost his appeal in 1931. He also issued Puffin stamps, which are still printed for the island today.

setup: When Martin Coles Harman, the self-styled 'King of Lundy', gave land in Surrey to the National Trust in 1926, he asked for it to be named...
detail: Harman himself had six brothers. He bought Lundy in 1925 for £25,000 and kept it despite later bankruptcy because it was held in trust.

setup: On 30 December 1952, Tower Bridge began to open while a number 78 double-decker bus was crossing it. The driver, Albert Gunter, responded by...
detail: The bus dropped onto the other half of the bridge with 20 passengers aboard. Gunter was given £10 and a day off as a reward.
source_title: Tower Bridge: The day a bus jumped over Tower Bridge

setup: On 5 April 1968, RAF Flight Lieutenant Alan Pollock made headlines when he flew his Hawker Hunter jet...
answer: straight through the middle of Tower Bridge
detail: He passed between the road deck and the high walkways. Other stunts there include a 1912 hydroplane flight and a 2024 wingsuit flight.
source_title: Tower Bridge: Daring feats at Tower Bridge

setup: In 1311, when its central spire was completed, the tallest building on Earth was no longer the Great Pyramid of Giza but...
detail: The pyramid had held the title for nearly 4,000 years. Lincoln kept it for over 200 years until the spire blew down in a storm in the mid-1500s.
source_title: History Revealed: What overtook the Great Pyramid?

setup: The Monument to the Great Fire of London was designed by Christopher Wren and Robert Hooke to double as...
answer: a giant telescope with a laboratory underneath
detail: A hidden lab below the column was meant for a zenith telescope looking straight up the shaft. Traffic vibrations from Fish Street Hill ruined the readings.
source_title: Londonist: The Secret Laboratory Inside The Monument

setup: The Monument to the Great Fire of London is exactly 202 feet tall, a figure chosen because...
answer: it's 202 feet from where the fire started
detail: Laid on its side, the column would reach Thomas Farriner's bakery on Pudding Lane. A narrow spiral of 311 steps leads to the viewing platform.
source_title: Wikipedia: Monument to the Great Fire of London

setup: The last person to live in Quay House in Conwy, the smallest house in Great Britain, was a fisherman called Robert Jones who was...
detail: The house's floor area is about 3 by 1.8 metres, so he could not stand up straight inside. He moved out in 1900 when the council declared it unfit to live in.
source_title: Wikipedia: Smallest House in Great Britain

setup: The London Necropolis Railway carried mourners and coffins from Waterloo to Brookwood Cemetery. Mourners bought return tickets, while the dead were given...
detail: The coffins also travelled in first, second or third class. The line ran from the 1850s until its London station was bombed in the Second World War.

setup: A small plaster nose sticks out from the inside of Admiralty Arch. Legend says it mocks Napoleon, but it was actually put there in 1997 by an artist protesting...
detail: Rick Buckley stuck casts of his own nose on buildings around London. He never publicised the prank, so myths about the noses grew up.

setup: The scheduled Loganair flight between the Orkney islands of Westray and Papa Westray is the shortest in the world. Its record-fastest crossing took...
detail: The islands are about 1.7 miles apart. The record was set by pilot Stuart Linklater, who flew the route more than 12,000 times.
source_title: Wikipedia: Westray to Papa Westray flight

setup: In 1885 a young woman named Sarah Ann Henley fell nearly 75 metres from Bristol's Clifton Suspension Bridge into the Avon Gorge. Remarkably, she...
answer: survived and lived to the age of 85
detail: She landed in thick mud at low tide. Witnesses credited her billowing skirt with slowing her fall, though that is uncertain. She married in 1900 and died in 1948.

setup: On Dorset's Isle of Portland, an old superstition says the word 'rabbit' brings bad luck, so locals call them 'furry things' or...
detail: Burrowing rabbits were blamed for rockfalls in the quarries. Quarrymen who spotted one would go home for the day.

setup: Because of a local taboo on the Isle of Portland, posters there for the 2005 film 'Wallace and Gromit: The Curse of the Were-Rabbit' replaced the title with...
detail: Islanders believe saying 'rabbit' can cause quarry collapses. The mayor said the word brings an awkward hush to any room.

setup: Hull is the only part of the UK never to have had red telephone boxes. Instead, its phone boxes are...
detail: Hull Corporation bought its local telephone network in 1914 for £192,423 and ran it independently of the Post Office. It now trades as KCOM.
source_title: The Telephone Box: Kiosk No 6 'Hull Corporation'

setup: The famous black bricks of 10 Downing Street are really...
answer: yellow, painted black to look like the old soot
detail: Restorers in the 1960s found centuries of pollution had blackened them. To keep the familiar look, the cleaned bricks were painted black.

setup: In 1908 Prime Minister H. H. Asquith had the famous front door of 10 Downing Street painted...
detail: It went back to black when his time in office ended in 1916. The house was also originally numbered 5 before being renumbered in the 18th century.
source_title: History Revealed: Facts about No 10 Downing Street

setup: In 1786 a surgeon removed a cyst from William Pitt the Younger's face inside 10 Downing Street. Afterwards Pitt's only complaint was...
answer: it took half a minute longer than promised
detail: The surgeon had estimated six minutes. It is the only known operation performed at No 10.
source_title: History Revealed: Facts about No 10 Downing Street

setup: When Ramsay MacDonald moved into 10 Downing Street in 1924, the house had no cutlery, crockery or bedsheets, so his daughter Ishbel...
answer: went shopping in the January sales
detail: Prime ministers were expected to supply their own furnishings. By 1846 the neighbourhood reportedly had 170 brothels and 145 gin parlours.
source_title: History Revealed: Facts about No 10 Downing Street

setup: Harold Wilson reported seeing a ghost in the private flat at 10 Downing Street. He described it as...
detail: His cleaner separately said she had seen the same figure in the private flat.
source_title: History Revealed: Facts about No 10 Downing Street

setup: In December 1976, a giant inflatable pig being photographed above Battersea Power Station for a Pink Floyd album cover broke free and ended up...
answer: scaring cows on a farm in Kent
detail: It drifted through Heathrow's flight paths first. A marksman hired to shoot it down if it escaped had not been told to come back for the second day.

setup: The signs for the Aberdeenshire hamlet of Lost were stolen so often that the council proposed renaming it...
detail: Locals objected, so instead the council put up a sign welded to its post in 2004. The name comes from Gaelic for 'inn'.

setup: After years of prank calls, stolen signs and tourists mooning for photos, residents of Butt Hole Road in Conisbrough, South Yorkshire, renamed it in 2009 to...
detail: Residents believe the old name came from a communal water butt. They raised £300 themselves to pay for the new sign.

setup: For years, residents of Bolinas in California have kept tourists away from their seaside town by...
answer: tearing down the road signs that point to it
detail: When county officials put the issue to a ballot, voters said they wanted no more signs.

setup: US Route 666, known as the 'Devil's Highway', got its unlucky number in 1926 simply because...
answer: it was the sixth branch off Route 66
detail: After years of stolen signs and talk of a curse, it was renumbered US 491 in 2003.

setup: Because the marker at mile 420 on Colorado's Interstate 70 kept getting stolen by cannabis fans, in 2014 it was replaced with a sign reading...
detail: The number 420 is slang for cannabis, which made the original marker a prized souvenir. The new sign was meant to be far less tempting.

setup: In 2011, Fort Wayne in Indiana held a public vote to name its new government building. The runaway winner, which officials quickly dropped, was...
detail: Baals was a former mayor whose name he pronounced 'balls'. It won 23,826 votes, and the building became Citizens Square.

setup: Before it changed its name in 1814, the Pennsylvania village of Intercourse was called...
detail: That was the name of a local tavern. The nearby Pennsylvania Dutch country also has places called Blue Ball and Bird-in-Hand.

setup: The village of Climax in Michigan got its name in 1834 when a settler climbed a tree, looked at the prairie and declared...
answer: 'This caps the climax of everything we saw'
detail: Daniel Eldred's family had searched for months for good farmland. In 1896 Climax became the first place in Michigan to get free rural mail delivery.

setup: Since 2017, the German village of Wacken, home to a huge heavy-metal festival, has kept fans supplied through...
detail: It can pour 10,000 litres an hour. The village has only about 2,000 residents, and every one of them gets free entry to the festival.

setup: Since 2013, the organisers of Germany's Wacken metal festival have promised that if the average noise level goes over 70 decibels they will...
detail: During the festival the village church also becomes a 'Metal Church'.

setup: A Penny Lane street sign taken from Liverpool in 1976 by a group of drunk students was finally returned...
detail: It is now on display at The Beatles Story museum. Signs were stolen so often that the city once simply painted the name on walls.

setup: Stoner Avenue in Bemidji, Minnesota lost its signs about 15 times a year. Residents refused to rename it, so the city...
answer: moved the signs onto ten-foot-tall poles
detail: The thefts had cost the city more than $20,000 in a decade. Residents rejected the alternative name Franklin Avenue in 2001.
source_title: Mental Floss: 10 Commonly Stolen Street Signs

setup: In 2012, NASA gave the name of a Canadian city, Yellowknife, to...
answer: the patch of Mars where the Curiosity rover landed
detail: Yellowknife is capital of the Northwest Territories. In the Dogrib language its name translates as 'where the money is'.

setup: Ulm Minster in Germany was the tallest church in the world from 1890. Its builders achieved this by deliberately making it...
answer: a few metres taller than Cologne Cathedral
detail: Its spire reaches 161.5 metres. Cologne, finished in 1880, had briefly held the title of world's tallest building.
source_title: Wikipedia: List of tallest church buildings

setup: The Chrysler Building held the title of world's tallest building for just eleven months. It snatched the title by...
answer: secretly assembling its spire so rivals couldn't respond
detail: The spire was 185 feet long, and it made the Chrysler the first building to pass 1,000 feet. The Empire State Building overtook it in 1931.
source_title: Mental Floss: 7 Surprising Buildings That Were Once World's Tallest

setup: After their village became the setting of a hit TV sketch show, the Dutch village of Maaskantje lost every one of its signs to souvenir hunters, so the council...
answer: decided not to replace them at all
detail: Fans of the comedy series New Kids, whose characters often pose by the village sign, took them all by 2009.

setup: According to one local story, the town of Hell in Michigan got its name when founder George Reeves was asked what to call it and replied...
answer: they could call it Hell for all he cared
detail: The name became official in 1841. Reeves reportedly also hid whiskey barrels from tax agents by sinking them in his millpond.

setup: Hell in Michigan is a well-known tourist stop, but the US Postal Service does not recognise it, so letters to Hell must be addressed to...
detail: Hell has no legal boundaries or official population. A journalist counted 76 residents in 2012.

setup: Westward Ho! got its name from a Charles Kingsley novel, but the phrase itself began as...
answer: a shout used by Thames boatmen to find passengers
detail: Watermen in the 16th century called 'Eastward ho!' and 'Westward ho!' to say which way they were going. Before the resort, the area was called Northam Burrows.

setup: At the London Necropolis Railway's Waterloo station, third-class mourners had to wait behind an opaque glass screen so that they...
answer: were hidden from the view of first- and second-class passengers
detail: Steam-powered lifts raised the coffins up to the platform, with first-class coffins loaded first. Carriage doors carried the names of the dead to keep funeral parties apart.
source_title: London Walking Tours: London Necropolis Railway

setup: In 1879, chemist Constantin Fahlberg discovered saccharin after noticing that...
answer: his dinner tasted sweet because of chemicals on his hands
detail: Fahlberg found an unexplained sweetness on his food, hands and arms even after washing, and traced it by tasting his lab equipment.

setup: In 2009, part of the Large Hadron Collider overheated because of...
answer: a piece of baguette, thought to have been dropped by a bird
detail: Bread on the surface electrical equipment let part of the circuit warm to almost 8 K, against a normal 1.9 K. Beams were not running at the time.

setup: In 18th-century London, kits were placed along the Thames to revive drowning victims by...
answer: blowing tobacco smoke up their bottoms
detail: The society that became the Royal Humane Society, founded in 1774, promoted the method. Doubts grew in the 1780s, and nicotine was shown to be toxic by 1811.
source_title: Science Museum blog: Saving lives with a puff of smoke

setup: In 1816, René Laennec invented the stethoscope because he was...
answer: too embarrassed to put his ear to a young woman's chest
detail: He rolled sheets of paper into a tube, pressed it to her chest and heard her heart more clearly than by ear. He later made a wooden version.
source_title: British Society for the History of Medicine

setup: The spacesuits worn on the Moon by Apollo astronauts were sewn by a company best known for making...
detail: International Latex Corporation, linked to Playtex, built the suits in Delaware. Many of its seamstresses had previously worked on underwear.

setup: During the 1969 Apollo 10 mission, the crew's recorded conversation includes an argument about...
answer: whose poo was floating around the cabin
detail: Commander Tom Stafford asked for a napkin to catch it. John Young and Gene Cernan both denied it was theirs.

setup: A 2018 Oxford-led study found that the cloud tops of Uranus are mostly made of...
answer: the gas that makes rotten eggs smell
detail: Patrick Irwin's team used the Gemini North telescope in Hawaii to detect hydrogen sulphide just above the clouds.

setup: Astronomers searching a giant dust cloud near the centre of our galaxy found ethyl formate, a chemical that gives flavour to...
detail: Arnaud Belloche of the Max Planck Institute for Radio Astronomy led the work, using the IRAM 30-metre telescope in southern Spain.

setup: The first human remains to reach the Moon belonged to planetary geologist Eugene Shoemaker, whose ashes were...
answer: carried by a NASA probe deliberately crashed into it
detail: About an ounce of his ashes flew on Lunar Prospector, launched in 1998 and crashed near the lunar south pole in 1999. Addison's disease had stopped him becoming an Apollo astronaut.

setup: After returning from the Moon in 1969, the Apollo 11 crew had to sign...
answer: a customs form declaring moon rocks and moon dust
detail: The form was filed at Honolulu Airport. It listed the departure point as Cape Kennedy, with a stop on the Moon. NASA called it a little joke at the time.

setup: To prove that bacteria cause stomach ulcers, Australian doctor Barry Marshall...
answer: drank a broth of the bacteria himself
detail: He developed gastritis within days in 1984. He shared the 2005 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Robin Warren.

setup: In 1929, a young German doctor pushed a 65cm tube up a vein in his own arm, then...
answer: walked to the X-ray room to photograph it in his heart
detail: Werner Forssmann's self-experiment pioneered cardiac catheterisation. He later became a urologist and shared the 1956 Nobel Prize.

setup: In 1804, a medical student tried to prove yellow fever wasn't contagious by...
answer: drinking the black vomit of patients
detail: Stubbins Ffirth of the University of Pennsylvania also rubbed it into cuts and his eye and suffered no ill effects. Yellow fever is spread by mosquitoes.

setup: In 1961, Soviet doctor Leonid Rogozov was the only surgeon at an Antarctic station when he...
detail: The roughly two-hour operation took place at Novolazarevskaya Station on 1 May 1961. The 27-year-old was assisted by a driver and a meteorologist, who held a mirror and passed instruments.

setup: After trying Humphry Davy's laughing gas in 1799, the poet Robert Southey declared that heaven's atmosphere must be...
detail: Davy tested nitrous oxide on himself and friends, including Samuel Taylor Coleridge, who ended one trial stamping on the ground in ecstasy.

setup: When Wilhelm Röntgen showed his wife the first X-ray of a human hand, hers, she said...
detail: The image, made on 22 December 1895, showed the bones of her hand and her wedding ring.

setup: In 1737, when Galileo's body was moved to a new tomb in Florence, admirers...
answer: cut off his middle finger as a relic
detail: It is displayed in a glass case at the Museo Galileo. His thumb, index finger and a tooth vanished after 1905 and resurfaced at auction in 2009.

setup: From 1898, the drug company Bayer sold heroin as...
answer: a cough medicine, even advertised for children
detail: It was promoted as a safe, non-addictive alternative to morphine. Bayer kept producing it until 1913.

setup: In the 1830s, Americans bought 'tomato pills', sold as a pure extract of tomato, which turned out to contain...
detail: Dr A.J. Holcombe launched them in 1835. Doctor John Cook Bennett had promoted tomatoes, even as 'catsup', as a treatment for diarrhoea and indigestion.

setup: Japanese researchers found in 2009 that the human body gives off visible light, and it glows brightest at...
detail: The glow is about 1,000 times weaker than the human eye can detect. The study was published in PLoS ONE.

setup: Andre Geim was the first person to win both a Nobel Prize and an Ig Nobel Prize as an individual. He won the Ig Nobel for...
detail: His Ig Nobel came in 2000, shared with Sir Michael Berry. His 2010 Nobel Prize in Physics was for work on graphene.

setup: Doctor Donald Unger spent over 60 years cracking the knuckles of only one hand, to test whether...
detail: He compared his left hand to his uncracked right. Neither got arthritis, and he won a 2009 Ig Nobel Prize.

setup: Two US doctors won a 2018 Ig Nobel Prize for showing that kidney stones can be dislodged by...
detail: They took a model of the kidney on Big Thunder Mountain Railroad at Walt Disney World. The idea came from a patient who passed a stone after a ride.

setup: In 2017, a physicist won an Ig Nobel Prize for using fluid dynamics to ask whether a cat is...
answer: both a solid and a liquid
detail: Marc-Antoine Fardin calculated how quickly cats take the shape of their containers.

setup: A 2019 Ig Nobel Prize in physics went to scientists who worked out how wombats produce...
detail: Dissections showed the cubes form inside the intestine, which has stiffer and softer sections, not at the exit. The team included Patricia Yang, David Hu and Scott Carver.

setup: A 2018 Ig Nobel-winning study showed that trained wine experts can detect, by smell alone...
answer: a single fly in a glass of wine
detail: Paul Becher and colleagues from five countries shared the biology prize.

setup: Portuguese conservators won a 2018 Ig Nobel Prize for showing that a good way to clean paintings and gilded sculptures is...
detail: They found saliva works as an effective cleaning agent, but warned against using it on kitchen counters.

setup: A British archaeologist won a 2018 Ig Nobel Prize for calculating that, compared with mammoth or horse, eating humans...
detail: James Cole concluded that cannibalism was a poor source of nutrition compared with many traditional meat diets.

setup: A 2017 Ig Nobel Prize went to researchers who found the first evidence that the hairy-legged vampire bat drinks...
detail: Fernanda Ito, Enrico Bernard and Rodrigo Torres won the nutrition prize.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: French neuroscientists won a 2017 Ig Nobel Prize for using brain scans to study people who are disgusted by...
detail: They found reward circuits in the brain switch off when these people look at food they find disgusting.

setup: A 2016 Ig Nobel Prize in physics explained why horseflies avoid white horses and why dragonflies are drawn to...
detail: Gábor Horváth and colleagues shared the physics prize.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: German researchers won a 2016 Ig Nobel Prize for showing that an itch on your left arm can be relieved by...
answer: scratching your right arm while looking in a mirror
detail: Christoph Helmchen and colleagues published the work in PLoS ONE in 2013.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: Chemists won a 2015 Ig Nobel Prize for inventing a way to partially...
detail: Callum Ormonde, Colin Raston and colleagues published their method in ChemBioChem in 2015.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: A 2015 Ig Nobel-winning study found that almost all mammals, whatever their size, take about 21 seconds to...
detail: Patricia Yang, David Hu and colleagues published the finding in PNAS in 2014.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: British doctors won a 2015 Ig Nobel Prize for showing that appendicitis can be diagnosed by asking patients whether it hurt...
detail: Diallah Karim, Anthony Harnden and colleagues published the study in the BMJ in 2012.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: Researcher Michael Smith shared a 2015 Ig Nobel Prize for mapping the most painful places to be stung by a honeybee, using...
detail: He shared the prize with Justin Schmidt, creator of the Schmidt Sting Pain Index.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: To understand how dinosaurs walked, scientists who won a 2015 Ig Nobel Prize...
answer: strapped weighted artificial tails onto chickens
detail: Bruno Grossi, José Iriarte-Díaz and colleagues published the study in PLoS ONE in 2014.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: Japanese researchers won a 2014 Ig Nobel Prize for measuring exactly how slippery it is to step on...
detail: Kiyoshi Mabuchi and colleagues measured the friction between shoe, banana skin and floor.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: A 2014 Ig Nobel Prize in neuroscience went to scientists who studied the brains of people who see...
answer: the face of Jesus in toast
detail: Jiangang Liu, Kang Lee and colleagues published the work in the journal Cortex in 2014.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: A 2014 Ig Nobel-winning study found that when dogs go to the toilet, they prefer to...
answer: line up with Earth's north-south magnetic field
detail: Vlastimil Hart, Hynek Burda and colleagues published the findings in Frontiers in Zoology in 2013.
source_title: Improbable Research: Ig Nobel past winners

setup: Japanese runner Shizo Kanakuri dropped out of the 1912 Stockholm Olympic marathon and went home without telling anyone. He officially crossed the finish line...
answer: in 1967, giving a time of over 54 years
detail: Swedish television invited him back aged 75 to finish the course. His official time was 54 years, 8 months, 6 days, 5 hours, 32 minutes and 20.3 seconds.

setup: Overheating in the 1912 Olympic marathon, Shizo Kanakuri left the course and spent about an hour...
answer: drinking orange juice at a stranger's garden party
detail: Embarrassed, he quietly travelled back to Japan, and Swedish officials treated him as a missing person for decades.

setup: At the 1912 Olympics, a Greco-Roman wrestling semi-final between Martin Klein and Alfred Asikainen lasted...
detail: It was held outdoors in the sun and Klein finally pinned his opponent. It is still described as the longest wrestling match on record.

setup: After winning an 11-hour wrestling bout at the 1912 Olympics, Martin Klein settled for silver because...
answer: he was too exhausted to wrestle in the final
detail: Russian doctors ruled him unfit, so Sweden's Claes Johanson took gold by default and the beaten Asikainen got bronze.
source_title: Britannica: The Match That Wouldn't End

setup: Scotsman Wyndham Halswelle won the 1908 Olympic 400 metres gold in unique circumstances, because in the final he was...
answer: the only runner on the track
detail: The first final was voided after an American was ruled to have obstructed him. The other two Americans boycotted the rerun, so Halswelle ran alone in about 50 seconds: the only walkover in Olympic track and field.

setup: Two Japanese pole vaulters tied at the 1936 Olympics and were given silver and bronze. Back home, they had a jeweller...
answer: cut both medals in half and fuse them together
detail: Shuhei Nishida and Sueo Oe each ended up with a half-silver, half-bronze medal, now known as the 'Medals of Friendship'.

setup: Melbourne hosted the 1956 Olympics, but the horse-riding events were held five months earlier in...
detail: Australia's strict six-month quarantine on imported horses made it impossible to hold them in Melbourne, so the IOC moved them to Sweden.
source_title: Wikipedia: Equestrian events at the 1956 Olympics

setup: At the separate 1956 equestrian Olympics in Stockholm, even the Olympic flame was...
answer: carried into the stadium on horseback
detail: Hans Wikne rode in with the flame and lit the torch, every competitor and flag bearer entered on their mount, and the athletes' oath was recited from the saddle.

setup: The 1900 Paris Olympics featured live pigeon shooting. Leon de Lunden of Belgium won the main event by bringing down...
detail: Shooters were out after missing two birds and nearly 300 pigeons died. The IOC doesn't count it among official results, but it's the only time animals were killed on purpose at the Games.

setup: In 1912, the Olympic gold medal for literature went to an 'Ode to Sport' entered under false names. The real author was...
answer: Pierre de Coubertin, founder of the modern Olympics
detail: He entered under the pseudonyms Georges Hohrod and M. Eschbach. Arts competitions awarded Olympic medals until 1948.

setup: The poet Robert Graves entered the 1924 Olympic literature competition. He lost and described the contest as...
detail: Olympic arts medals were awarded between 1912 and 1948. That same year Jack Butler Yeats won a silver for painting.

setup: Avery Brundage, who later ran the International Olympic Committee, entered the Olympic literature contest twice and managed...
detail: He received the first ever honourable mention in literature in 1932. As IOC president he later opposed the arts competitions.

setup: In the entire history of the Olympic arts competitions, the number of medals ever awarded for drama was...
detail: Lauro de Bosis won silver for a dramatic work in 1928. No medals were given for drama in 1936 or 1948.

setup: Fred Lorz crossed the line first in the 1904 Olympic marathon to loud cheers, until it emerged that...
answer: he'd covered about ten miles of it in a car
detail: Lorz got cramp, accepted a lift, then rejoined when the car broke down. He confessed, was banned for life, and was later reinstated.

setup: On the way to the 1904 St Louis Olympics, Cuban marathon runner Félix Carvajal lost all his money...
answer: gambling on dice in New Orleans
detail: He then walked and hitched his way to St Louis. He still finished fourth in the marathon.

setup: South African runner Len Taunyane might have finished higher than ninth in the 1904 Olympic marathon, but he was...
answer: chased about a mile off course by a dog
detail: He and Jan Mashiani were the first Black Africans to compete at the Olympics. A dog drove him about a mile off the route, yet he still finished ninth.

setup: In the 1904 Olympic marathon, American runner William Garcia nearly died from internal bleeding caused by...
answer: breathing in dust thrown up by officials' cars
detail: Officials' cars drove along the dirt roads beside the runners. Garcia was found unconscious on the course with severe internal injuries.

setup: American gymnast George Eyser won six Olympic medals in a single day in 1904, despite...
detail: He lost his left leg as a child when a train ran over it. He won three golds, two silvers and a bronze, including in rope climbing.

setup: The 200m swimming race at the 1900 Paris Olympics was held in the River Seine, and competitors had to...
answer: climb over boats and swim under others
detail: Swimmers clambered over a pole and a row of boats, then dived under another row. Australia's Frederick Lane won in 2:38.4 and the event was never held again.

setup: The 1900 Olympics included an underwater swimming race where competitors scored points for distance and also for...
detail: It was held in the Seine and only ever staged once. Swimmers got two points per metre and one per second underwater; the best managed 60 metres.

setup: For winning the women's golf at the 1900 Olympics, Margaret Abbott received no medal. Her prize was...
detail: It was an old Saxon porcelain bowl mounted in gold, with no sign it was an Olympic prize.

setup: In the same 1900 Olympic golf event that Margaret Abbott won, another competitor who finished well down the field was...
detail: Mary Abbott shot a 65 and tied for seventh. They're described as the only mother and daughter to compete in the same Olympic event at the same time.

setup: The golf course for the 1900 Paris Olympics was laid out...
detail: It had tiny 'postage stamp' greens. Olympic golf vanished after 1904 and didn't return for 112 years.

setup: In the 1900 Olympic croquet tournament, the number of paying spectators was reportedly...
detail: Only French players entered, so France won every event. Croquet has never returned to the Olympics.
source_title: NPR: Live Pigeon Shooting And Other Odd Olympic Games

setup: At the 1900 Paris Olympics, a Belgian horse called Extra Dry won gold in...
answer: the long jump, with a leap of 6.10 metres
detail: Ridden by Constant van Langhendonck, it won an equestrian long jump that was only ever held once. There was also a high jump for horses.

setup: In the 1904 Olympic 'plunge for distance', competitors dived into the water and then had to...
answer: glide face down without moving for up to a minute
detail: Distance was measured after 60 seconds or when their head came up. William Dickey won with 62 feet 6 inches (19.05 m); all five entrants were American and it was never held again.

setup: Swedish shooter Oscar Swahn won an Olympic silver medal in 1920 at the age of...
detail: He shot in the running deer event, having won gold at 64 in 1912. His son Alf competed alongside him.
source_title: Olympiaddenda: RIP to these defunct Olympic sports

setup: In the 1908 Olympic tug of war, all three medal-winning teams were...
detail: Americans complained that the Liverpool police wore heavy boots, but the protest was overruled.
source_title: Olympiaddenda: RIP to these defunct Olympic sports

setup: In the 1912 Olympic tug of war final, Great Britain lost to Sweden after two members of the London team...
answer: sat down on the ground, which broke the rules
detail: Accounts differ on whether they were exhausted or seeking leverage, but Sweden was awarded the pull. Tug of war last appeared at the Olympics in 1920.
source_title: Olympiaddenda: RIP to these defunct Olympic sports

setup: At the 1900 Paris Olympics there was no proper running track, and the hurdles were made from...
detail: Athletics was held on bumpy grassland with trees dotted about. Despite this, Alvin Kraenzlein won four individual titles.
source_title: The weirdness of the 1900 Paris Olympics

setup: Basque pelota was an official Olympic sport only once, in 1900. Spain won gold because...
answer: France, the only other team, pulled out
detail: The French withdrew over a rules dispute before a ball was struck, so Spain won by default.
source_title: The weirdness of the 1900 Paris Olympics

setup: The idea of athletes mingling together at the Olympic closing ceremony instead of marching by nation came from...
detail: John Ian Wing wrote anonymously to organisers just before the 1956 closing ceremony suggesting athletes mingle instead of marching behind flags. It has been tradition ever since.

setup: During the 1956 Olympic torch relay, the Mayor of Sydney was fooled into accepting a fake torch made from...
answer: a chair leg, a plum pudding tin and kerosene-soaked underpants
detail: Sydney University students built it as a prank and veterinary student Barry Larkin ran it in. The mayor made his speech before someone whispered that it was a hoax.

setup: With only about 5,000 TV sets in Australia during the 1956 Melbourne Olympics, many people watched it...
answer: at petrol stations and community halls
detail: Local stations agreed to televise the Games just a week before they started, and overseas broadcasters got no rights.

setup: The 1956 Melbourne Games remain the only Summer Olympics held in...
detail: They were timed to fall in the southern hemisphere's spring and early summer. They were also the first Games held in the southern hemisphere.

setup: Melbourne won the 1949 vote to host the 1956 Olympics by a margin of...
detail: Problems with preparations later led IOC president Avery Brundage to suggest Rome might take over.

setup: An Olympic romance at the height of the Cold War saw American hammer thrower Hal Connolly...
detail: He married Olga Fikotová, who later competed for the United States and carried the US flag in 1972.

setup: The 1956 Olympic water polo match between Hungary and the Soviet Union, just after the Hungarian uprising, ended with...
answer: police stepping in to stop a near riot
detail: Known as the 'Blood in the Water' match, it was stopped early with Hungary 4-0 up. Hungary went on to win gold.

setup: Monopoly began as 'The Landlord's Game', patented by Lizzie Magie in 1904 with the aim of...
answer: showing the evils of landlords and monopolies
detail: Magie wanted to show how piling up property enriches a few and impoverishes everyone else.

setup: Lizzie Magie, who invented the forerunner of Monopoly, was paid by Parker Brothers for her patent a total of...
detail: Salesman Charles Darrow, who sold Parker Brothers a copied version, became famous as Monopoly's 'inventor'.

setup: To protest about women's position in society, Monopoly's original inventor Lizzie Magie placed a newspaper advert...
answer: offering herself for sale as a 'young woman American slave'
detail: She offered herself to be auctioned off to a husband to highlight women's position. The stunt was reported in news and gossip columns nationwide.

setup: Before inventing the game that became Monopoly, Lizzie Magie's day job was as a typist at...
answer: the Dead Letter Office in Washington
detail: She was also a poet, short-story writer and actor.

setup: In Lizzie Magie's 1904 'Landlord's Game', the corner square that sent you to jail belonged to...
detail: Parker Brothers later pulled Magie's 1939 edition of the game and destroyed almost all the unsold copies.

setup: In the Second World War, British intelligence had Monopoly sets made for prisoners of war with hidden...
answer: silk escape maps, compasses and real money
detail: Waddingtons of Leeds hid the items in recesses in the board, with real German or Italian banknotes among the play money.

setup: Play-Doh was turned from a cleaning product into a toy after being suggested by...
detail: Kay Zufall persuaded Joseph McVicker in 1955 to sell it as a toy.
source_title: The Strong National Museum of Play

setup: During the Vietnam War, US soldiers used metal Slinkys as...
detail: Stretched out and hung up, a metal Slinky made a handy portable antenna in the field.

setup: When Mr Potato Head went on sale in 1952, one thing the box didn't include was...
detail: Children pushed the spiked plastic features into a real potato or other vegetable. The plastic body wasn't added until 1964, after parents complained about rotting vegetables.

setup: In 1952, Mr Potato Head made advertising history by becoming...
answer: the first toy ever advertised on television
detail: It was also the first advert aimed directly at children, encouraging them to pester their parents.

setup: In the 1985 election for mayor of Boise, Idaho, the candidate Mr Potato Head received...
detail: Guinness verified it as the most votes ever cast for Mr Potato Head in a political campaign.

setup: In 1987, Mr Potato Head joined an anti-smoking campaign by handing the US Surgeon General his...
detail: He was made the 'Spokespud' for the Great American Smokeout and gave up his pipe to C. Everett Koop in Washington.

setup: Before Hasbro got hold of it, the rights to Mr Potato Head were briefly bought by a breakfast cereal company planning to...
answer: give the face parts away free in cereal boxes
detail: Post Cereals bought inventor George Lerner's 'Funny Face Man' in 1951. Hasbro bought it back a few months later.

setup: In medieval English, calling someone 'nice' was no compliment. The word originally meant...
detail: It comes via French from Latin 'nescius', 'not knowing' (ne- 'not' plus scire 'to know'). The pleasant modern sense only developed centuries later.
source_title: NPR: Word of the Week, nice

setup: Long before it meant daft, the word 'silly' (once spelled 'seely') meant...
detail: It goes back to Old English 'gesælig', related to German 'selig' (blessed). It drifted through 'innocent', 'harmless' and 'pitiable' before meaning foolish in the 1570s.

setup: Before it named a dark German rye bread, 'pumpernickel' was an insult for an oaf. It combines two words roughly meaning...
detail: 'Pumpern' meant to break wind and 'Nickel' (from Nicholas) a goblin or rascal. The tale that Napoleon named it after his horse is a myth: the word predates him.

setup: The partridge gets its name, via Latin, from the Greek 'perdix', which is probably linked to a Greek verb meaning...
detail: The likely reason is the whirring, rumbling noise the bird's wings make as it bursts into flight.

setup: In Hamlet, a schemer is 'hoist with his own petard'. A petard was a small bomb for blasting open gates, and its name comes from the French for...
detail: French 'pétard' comes from 'péter', to fart. 'Hoist' meant lifted into the air, so the phrase means blown up by your own bomb.

setup: 'Feisty' comes from 'feist', an American word for a small yappy dog. Before that, 'feist' or 'fist' meant...
detail: In the mid-1400s 'fist' meant breaking wind or a foul smell. An 1811 slang dictionary defined 'fice' as 'a small windy escape backwards'.

setup: When the verb 'fizzle' entered English in the 1530s, it had nothing to do with fireworks or fizzy drinks. It meant...
answer: to break wind without making a noise
detail: It probably grew from the obsolete word 'fist', a fart. The sense of a flop that 'fizzles out' arose in American college slang in the 1840s.

setup: 'Poppycock', meaning nonsense, probably came to America with Dutch settlers. In Dutch, the original was a rude word for...
detail: The likely source is Dutch 'poppekak', literally doll's dung, or dialect 'pappekak', soft food plus dung. Either way, 'kak' means excrement.

setup: The word 'muscle' comes from the Latin 'musculus', which literally means...
detail: Romans thought some muscles, especially the biceps, looked like mice moving under the skin. Greek 'mys' also meant both mouse and muscle, giving the medical prefix 'myo-'.

setup: Medieval English had another word for a muscle, 'lacerte', which came from the Latin word for...
detail: Like the mouse comparison behind 'muscle', the idea was of a small creature rippling beneath the skin.

setup: The explorer William Dampier, who introduced 'avocado' to English, also gave us the words...
detail: Dampier (1652-1715), a buccaneer turned naturalist, contributed over 1,000 words to English, including 'breadfruit' and 'tortilla'.

setup: The flower name 'orchid' comes from the Greek word 'orkhis', which means...
detail: The plant was named for the shape of its paired, rounded root tubers.

setup: The mould that gave us penicillin was named because, under a microscope, its spore-bearing branches looked like tiny...
detail: Latin 'penicillum' meant a paintbrush, and the same word is the source of English 'pencil'.

setup: Karel Čapek's 1920 play R.U.R. gave the world the word 'robot', but the word was actually thought up by...
detail: Karel had considered 'labori'. Josef suggested 'robota', Czech for forced labour, reportedly without taking the paintbrush out of his mouth.
source_title: Glagoslav: Who invented the word robot?

setup: The earliest known printed use of the word 'nerd' is in a 1950 children's book by...
detail: In If I Ran the Zoo, it is one of a list of imaginary creatures: 'a Nerkle, a Nerd, and a Seersucker, too!'
source_title: NPR: Nerd, Word of the Week

setup: In 1951, Newsweek reported that Detroit teenagers now called a square a 'nerd', or, in a milder case...
detail: The article was a round-up of modern teen slang. 'Nerd' survived; 'scurve' sank without trace.

setup: Horace Walpole coined 'serendipity' in a 1754 letter, after a fairy tale set in Serendip, an old name for...
detail: The tale was The Three Princes of Serendip, whose heroes kept discovering things they 'were not in quest of'. Walpole's letter wasn't published until 1833.

setup: Physicist Murray Gell-Mann had the sound 'kwork' in mind for his new particle, then found the spelling 'quark' in...
detail: The line is 'Three quarks for Muster Mark!' Gell-Mann imagined it as a pub call for 'three quarts', justifying his pronunciation. Three suited too: a proton needs three quarks.
source_title: Science Friday: The origin of the word quark

setup: The word 'googol', for a one followed by a hundred zeros, was invented by...
detail: Milton Sirotta suggested it to his uncle Edward Kasner, who popularised it in the 1940 book Mathematics and the Imagination.

setup: Young Milton Sirotta also named the googolplex, which he defined as a one followed by...
answer: as many zeros as you could write before collapsing
detail: His uncle, mathematician Edward Kasner, tidied it up to a one followed by a googol zeros.
source_title: Damn Interesting: A googol by any other name

setup: The word 'scientist' was first printed in 1834, in William Whewell's review of a book by...
detail: Whewell's anonymous review proposed 'scientist' by analogy with 'artist'. Until then the usual term was 'natural philosopher'.

setup: When William Whewell coined 'physicist', Michael Faraday said he could never bring himself to use it because...
detail: The new word irritated many; Blackwood's Magazine mocked its 'sibilant consonants that fizz like squib'.

setup: By 1899, English had a sneering offshoot of the word 'scientist': 'scientaster', meaning...
detail: 'Scientaster' dates from 1899, on the model of 'poetaster' for a bad poet. 'Scientician' (1885) also had a brief run.

setup: The word 'scientist' was first proposed at an 1833 Cambridge meeting, in reply to a complaint from the poet...
detail: Coleridge objected to fossil-diggers and electricity experimenters calling themselves 'natural philosophers'. William Whewell suggested 'scientist', by analogy with 'artist'.

setup: The 1975 New Columbia Encyclopedia featured Lillian Virginia Mountweazel, a photographer and fountain designer. She was in fact...
answer: a fake entry planted to catch copiers
detail: Fake reference entries are now nicknamed 'Mountweazels' in her honour, a term coined by New Yorker writer Henry Alford in 2005.

setup: The New Oxford American Dictionary defined 'esquivalience' as 'the wilful avoidance of one's official responsibilities'. The word was...
answer: invented by an editor to catch copiers
detail: Editor Christine Lindberg made it up to protect the dictionary's CD-ROM edition. New Yorker writer Henry Alford exposed it in 2005.

setup: The Devon village of Westward Ho!, the only British place name with an exclamation mark, was named after...
detail: Kingsley's 1855 bestseller was set in nearby Bideford. Developers formed a company in 1863 and even named their hotel the 'Westward Ho!-tel'.

setup: A 1903 music dictionary listed 'zzxjoanw' as a Māori word for a drum. It was exposed as a hoax because...
answer: Māori has no J, X or Z, and its words end in vowels
detail: It sat in Rupert Hughes's Musical Guide through editions up to 1939, until Philip Cohen flagged it in the magazine Word Ways in 1976.

setup: In 2008, people noticed Google Maps showing a Lancashire town called Argleton, which was actually...
detail: Some websites even listed businesses and weather for Argleton. Google's data supplier couldn't explain it, and it was removed by May 2010.

setup: Since 1979, Germany's parliament has listed Jakob Maria Mierscheid as a Social Democrat MP, even though he...
detail: Two SPD members invented him. He has his own stationery and email address, and in 1983 'he' published a 'law' linking his party's vote to West German steel production.

setup: Georgia Tech student George P. Burdell, enrolled in 1927, earned two degrees and was even listed on a wartime bomber crew. He was...
answer: an imaginary student invented as a prank
detail: Student Ed Smith enrolled him after receiving two enrolment forms by mistake. In 1969 hackers signed Burdell up for every class, over 3,000 credit hours.

setup: A 1957 German book described 'snouters', mammals that walk on their noses, and explained nobody can study them now because...
answer: their islands sank after nuclear tests
detail: Zoologist Gerolf Steiner invented them under a fake name. Conveniently, every snouter researcher was supposedly at a conference on the islands when they sank.

setup: In 2010, Google planted about 100 nonsense search words like 'hiybbprqag', each linked to an unrelated page. Soon afterwards...
answer: nine of them turned up as top results on Bing
detail: Google used the made-up words as a trap, suspecting its rival of copying its results.

setup: Trivia author Fred L. Worth planted a fake fact in his book, then sued Trivial Pursuit for $300 million when...
answer: his invented first name for Columbo appeared in the game
detail: The case was dismissed because facts, even false ones, aren't protected by copyright.

setup: In 1985, people invented a Massachusetts town called Ripton to protest official ignorance of rural areas. It was so convincing that...
answer: the state gave it budget money and grants
detail: The hoax ran until it was revealed, by which time the made-up town had already received public funds.

setup: A famous French philosopher once quoted the thinker Jean-Baptiste Botul in a serious book, unaware that Botul...
detail: Frédéric Pagès and friends created Botul as a literary joke. The philosopher who fell for it was Bernard-Henri Lévy.

setup: The film guide The Golden Turkey Awards listed a movie called 'Dog of Norway', which starred...
detail: The film never existed. It featured 'Muki the Wonder Dog' and was planted as a challenge for readers to spot.

setup: For centuries, many English speakers used a different name for asparagus, reshaping it into familiar words:...
detail: A classic folk etymology: an unfamiliar Greek-derived word was bent into two everyday English ones, 'sparrow' and 'grass'.

setup: In Middle English, the snake we call 'an adder' was actually...
detail: People misheard 'a nadder' as 'an adder', and the N jumped across. The same thing happened to 'a napron', which became 'an apron'.

setup: The 'groom' in 'bridegroom' has nothing to do with stable lads. The Old English word 'brydguma' meant...
detail: When 'guma' (man) fell out of use, English swapped in the similar-sounding 'groom', which then meant a male servant.

setup: The small bird called the wheatear has nothing to do with wheat or ears. Its Middle English name meant...
detail: 'Whit-ers' was later reshaped into the more respectable-sounding 'wheatear', possibly out of politeness.

setup: A hangnail now means a torn bit of skin by a fingernail, but the Old English 'angnægl' originally meant...
answer: a painful corn on the foot
detail: The second part is Old English 'nægl', which here meant a hard corn, not a fingernail. Later speakers reinterpreted the word as a bit of nail that 'hangs'.

setup: 'Shamefaced' has nothing to do with faces. It was originally 'shamefast', meaning...
detail: 'Fast' meant fixed, as in 'stuck fast'. The ending was later reinterpreted as 'faced'.

setup: To 'curry favour' began as the Middle English phrase 'curry favel', meaning...
detail: To curry is to comb down a horse, and 'favel' was a chestnut horse. Once 'favel' was forgotten, people heard 'favour'.

setup: A 'forlorn hope' was originally a group of soldiers. It comes from Dutch 'verloren hoop', which means...
detail: It named the storming party sent first into a breach. English ears heard 'hope', giving the modern sense of a hopeless venture.

setup: The cockroach got its English name in the 1620s, when people reshaped the Spanish word...
detail: English speakers bent it to sound like two familiar words, 'cock' and 'roach'.

setup: The silent 's' in 'island' has never been pronounced, because it was only added...
detail: Old English had 'igland'. The s was inserted under the influence of 'isle', which comes from Latin 'insula' and isn't actually related.

setup: The phrase 'steal my thunder' comes from playwright John Dennis, who was furious when a production of Macbeth used...
detail: Dennis made thunder with a sheet of tin for his flop Appius and Virginia (1709). Hearing it reused, he reportedly cried: 'They will not let my play run, but they steal my thunder!'
source_title: Take Our Word For It: steal thunder
